Introduction

Skin appendages include hair follicles, sebaceous glands, sweat glands (eccrine & apocrine), and nails. Infections of these structures are common in clinical practice and range from superficial to deep, requiring different management.

1. Folliculitis

  • Definition — superficial inflammation of hair follicle; small (<5 mm) erythematous papules or pustules centred on hair follicle.
  • Causes — S. aureus (most common); Pseudomonas aeruginosa (hot tub folliculitis); Candida; Malassezia (Pityrosporum folliculitis); Molluscum contagiosum; herpes simplex; Gram-negative folliculitis (acne treatment).
  • Types — superficial (Bockhart's impetigo — S. aureus), deep, eosinophilic (Ofuji), Gram-negative, pityrosporum.
  • Clinical — itchy papules & pustules in hair-bearing areas (beard, scalp, axilla, buttocks, thighs).
  • Treatment — topical mupirocin, clindamycin, benzoyl peroxide; oral antibiotics for extensive (dicloxacillin, cephalexin); warm compresses.

2. Furuncle (Boil)

  • Definition — deep infection of hair follicle extending into subcutaneous tissue; painful, erythematous, fluctuant nodule with central necrotic plug (pustule).
  • Cause — S. aureus (>90%); MRSA increasing.
  • Sites — neck, face, axilla, buttocks, thighs, breast; often in adolescents & young adults.
  • Clinical — painful nodule enlarging over days; central yellow pustule ruptures, discharging pus & necrotic core; regional lymphadenitis.
  • Treatment — warm compresses (encourage spontaneous drainage); incision & drainage (I&D); dicloxacillin/cephalexin if surrounding cellulitis, fever, immunocompromised, or facial lesion.

3. Carbuncle

  • Definition — coalescence of multiple furuncles involving adjacent follicles, with drainage through multiple openings on skin surface.
  • Cause — S. aureus (including MRSA).
  • Sites — back of neck, shoulders, thighs, buttocks (thick skin); rare in face.
  • Clinical — larger, more painful than furuncle; systemic symptoms (fever, malaise); multiple draining sinuses; slower healing; scar formation.
  • Risk factors — diabetes, malnutrition, immunocompromise, obesity, poor hygiene.
  • Treatment — I&D + antibiotics (dicloxacillin/cephalexin; vancomycin if MRSA); control diabetes; treat carriers.

4. Hidradenitis Suppurativa (Acne Inversa)

  • Definition — chronic, recurrent, deep inflammation of apocrine sweat glands; painful nodules, abscesses, sinus tracts, scarring.
  • Sites — axillae, groin, buttocks, inframammary folds, perianal.
  • Cause — follicular occlusion → secondary bacterial infection (S. aureus, anaerobes, Streptococcus, Gram-negative bacilli); genetic predisposition.
  • Clinical — Hurley stages I (single/multiple abscesses, no sinus tracts/scars), II (recurrent abscesses with sinus tracts & scarring, single or multiple widely separated lesions), III (diffuse involvement with multiple interconnected tracts & abscesses).
  • Treatment — topical clindamycin; oral tetracycline/clindamycin + rifampin; adalimumab (anti-TNF — first FDA-approved biologic); surgery (wide local excision); lifestyle (weight loss, smoking cessation).

5. Sweat Gland Infections

  • Miliaria (heat rash / prickly heat)
    • Occlusion of eccrine sweat ducts; retention of sweat.
    • Types — Miliaria crystallina (superficial vesicles), Miliaria rubra (erythematous papules — "prickly heat"), Miliaria profunda (flesh-coloured papules — chronic).
    • Treatment — cooling, dry environment, calamine; secondary bacterial infection may require antibiotics.
  • Apocrine gland infection (hidradenitis suppurativa) — as above.

6. Nail & Nail Fold Infections

  • Paronychia
    • Infection of nail fold (proximal/lateral).
    • Acute — S. aureus (most common); painful, erythematous, fluctuant swelling; treatment — warm soaks, I&D if abscess, oral antibiotics (dicloxacillin).
    • Chronic — Candida albicans; dishwashers, bartenders, diabetics; boggy nail fold, nail dystrophy; treatment — topical antifungal (miconazole, clotrimazole), keep dry, oral itraconazole for refractory.
  • Felon
    • Deep infection of distal finger pulp.
    • Cause — S. aureus; puncture wound.
    • Clinical — severe throbbing pain, swelling, tense pulp; risk of necrosis & osteomyelitis.
    • Treatment — urgent I&D (lateral incision), oral antibiotics.
  • Onychomycosis (tinea unguium)
    • Fungal infection of nail plate.
    • Causes — Trichophyton rubrum (most common), T. mentagrophytes, Epidermophyton floccosum; Candida; non-dermatophyte moulds (Scopulariopsis, Aspergillus).
    • Types — distal subungual (most common), proximal subungual (HIV), white superficial, candidal, total dystrophic.
    • Treatment — oral terbinafine 250 mg OD × 6 weeks (fingernails) / 12 weeks (toenails); itraconazole pulse; topical efinaconazole, tavaborole for mild.
  • Herpetic whitlow
    • HSV-1 or HSV-2 infection of finger; painful vesicles; healthcare workers, children with oral HSV.
    • Treatment — oral acyclovir/valacyclovir; do NOT incise (delayed healing, secondary infection).

7. Hair & Sebaceous Gland Infections

  • Acne vulgaris
    • Disorder of pilosebaceous unit — increased sebum, keratin plug, Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes) colonisation, inflammation.
    • Comedones (open/closed), papules, pustules, nodules, cysts, scars.
    • Treatment — topical retinoids (adapalene, tretinoin), benzoyl peroxide, antibiotics (clindamycin), oral isotretinoin for severe.
  • Tinea capitis
    • Dermatophyte infection of hair shaft & scalp; Microsporum, Trichophyton.
    • Types — endothrix (within shaft — "black dot"), ectothrix (outside shaft), favus (crust + scutula).
    • Treatment — oral griseofulvin × 6–8 weeks; terbinafine, itraconazole; selenium sulphide shampoo.
  • Ringworm (tinea corporis, cruris, pedis)
    • Dermatophyte infection of keratinised skin; Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton.
    • Treatment — topical clotrimazole, miconazole, terbinafine; oral for extensive/recurrent.

Clinical Pearl

The single most important clinical decision in skin appendage infections is whether or not to drain an abscess — antibiotics alone cannot penetrate the abscess wall. Furuncles <5 mm can often drain spontaneously with warm compresses; larger lesions require I&D. Always suspect MRSA in recurrent skin abscesses, especially if there is a household contact with similar lesions, recent antibiotic use, hospitalisation, or sports team involvement. Send pus for culture & sensitivity — guide therapy. For recurrent furunculosis, address predisposing factors — diabetes, nasal carriage of S. aureus (decolonise with mupirocin), immunodeficiency, hygiene, nutrition. Herpetic whitlow must NOT be incised — it is viral, not bacterial, and I&D causes delayed healing & superinfection. Acne is not an infection — it is a disorder of the pilosebaceous unit; antibiotics are used for their anti-inflammatory effect, not antimicrobial — hence the rise of C. acnes antibiotic resistance and the move toward non-antibiotic therapies (benzoyl peroxide, retinoids, isotretinoin).

Introduction

Leprosy (Hansen's disease) is a chronic granulomatous infection of skin and peripheral nerves caused by Mycobacterium leprae or Mycobacterium lepromatosis. India accounts for ~60% of global leprosy cases despite elimination (prevalence <1/10,000) achieved in 2005.

Etiology

  • Mycobacterium leprae — acid-fast, obligate intracellular bacillus; cannot be cultured on artificial media or in cell culture (only in mouse footpad, armadillo, nude mouse).
  • Generation time — 12–14 days (slowest growing human bacterial pathogen).
  • Preference for cooler tissues — skin (especially ear lobes, eyebrows, cheeks), peripheral nerves (ulnar, posterior auricular, peroneal, posterior tibial), anterior eye, upper respiratory tract (nasal mucosa); avoids warm internal organs.
  • Uncultivable — diagnostic challenge; mouse footpad culture for research only.
  • M. lepromatosis — newly described species; causes diffuse lepromatous leprosy (Lucio phenomenon); mainly Mexico & Caribbean.
  • Transmission — prolonged close contact via nasal droplets (multibacillary cases); incubation 2–10 years (longest of any bacterial disease).
  • Host immunity determines disease spectrum — strong Th1 (cell-mediated) immunity → tuberculoid (paucibacillary) disease; weak Th1 / strong Th2 (humoral) → lepromatous (multibacillary) disease.

Clinical Manifestations — Ridley-Jopling Classification

Type Skin lesions Nerve involvement Bacillary load Immunity
Indeterminate (I)Single hypopigmented macule; vagueNone/minimalNegativeUnstable; early lesion
Tuberculoid (TT)Single/few well-defined anaesthetic hypopigmented plaque with raised edges; dry, hairlessMarked — one nerve thickened (great auricular, ulnar, peroneal)Negative/scantyStrong CMI (Th1)
Borderline tuberculoid (BT)Multiple asymmetric plaques, some satellite lesionsMultiple nervesScantyModerate CMI

Borderline lepromatous (BL)Numerous bilateral lesions; nodules, plaquesMultiple; glove-stocking anaesthesiaHighWeak CMI

WHO Operational Classification (for treatment)

  • Paucibacillary (PB) — 1–5 skin lesions; smear-negative; treated with MB-MDT 6 months (Rifampicin 600 mg monthly supervised + Dapsone 100 mg daily self-administered).
  • Multibacillary (MB) — >5 skin lesions or smear-positive; treated with MB-MDT 12 months (Rifampicin 600 mg + Clofazimine 300 mg monthly supervised + Dapsone 100 mg + Clofazimine 50 mg daily self-administered).

Reactions — Type 1 vs Type 2

  • Type 1 (Reversal reaction)
    • Delayed Type IV hypersensitivity; affects borderline (BT, BB, BL) leprosy.
    • Sudden inflammation of existing skin lesions — erythema, oedema, tenderness; acute neuritis.
    • Treatment — prednisolone 40–60 mg/day tapered over 12 weeks; NSAIDs; MDT continued.
  • Type 2 (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum — ENL)
    • Immune complex (Type III) reaction; affects lepromatous (LL, BL) leprosy.
    • Crops of painful erythematous nodules on face, extensor surfaces; fever, malaise, iritis, orchitis, neuritis, dactylitis, lymphadenitis, glomerulonephritis.
    • Treatment — thalidomide 100–300 mg/day (women of childbearing age — absolutely contraindicated, teratogenic); prednisolone; clofazimine increased to 300 mg/day; MDT continued.
  • Lucio phenomenon — diffuse lepromatous leprosy (M. lepromatosis); necrotising vasculitis with skin ulcerations; Mexico/Central America.

Neurological Involvement

  • Skin lesions anaesthetic — earliest & most reliable sign.
  • Nerve thickening — great auricular, ulnar (above elbow), radial cutaneous (wrist), common peroneal (knee), posterior tibial, sural.
  • Claw hand (ulnar); foot drop (peroneal); claw toes (tibial); lagophthalmos, corneal anaesthesia (facial).
  • Trophic ulcers (painless plantar ulcers), autoamputation, absorption of digits.

Laboratory Diagnosis

1. Clinical Diagnosis

  • Cardinal signs (WHO — 1 or more confirms leprosy):
    1. Hypopigmented/reddish skin lesion with definite loss of sensation.
    2. Thickened peripheral nerves with loss of sensation in area supplied.
    3. Skin smear positive for AFB.
  • Skin lesion — test sensation with wisp of cotton (light touch) & pinprick (pain); compare with normal skin.
  • Nerve examination — palpate for thickening & tenderness.

2. Skin Smear (Slit-Skin Smear)

  • Procedure — pinch skin fold between thumb & forefinger (to make bloodless); small incision (5 mm long, 3 mm deep) with sterile scalpel; scrape dermal tissue with blade edge; smear on slide; stain with Ziehl-Neelsen or Fite-Faraco (modified acid-fast — uses less strong decolouriser as M. leprae is less acid-fast than M. tuberculosis).
  • Sites — ear lobes (cooler, high yield), eyebrows, cheek, chin, extensor surfaces of limbs, edges of active lesions (6 sites total).
  • Grading — Ridley's logarithmic index (BI — Bacterial Index)
    • 0 = no bacilli in 100 oil-immersion fields.
    • 1+ = 1–10 bacilli per 100 fields.
    • 2+ = 1–10 bacilli per 10 fields.
    • 3+ = 1–10 bacilli per field.
    • 4+ = 10–100 bacilli per field.
    • 5+ = 100–1000 bacilli per field.
    • 6+ = >1000 bacilli per field (globi — clusters of bacilli in macrophages; pathognomonic of LL).
  • Morphological Index (MI) — percentage of solid-staining bacilli (live) vs fragmented (dead); used to monitor treatment response.
  • Sensitivity — high in LL, BL (multibacillary); low in TT, BT, indeterminate (paucibacillary) — usually smear-negative.

3. Skin Biopsy

  • Site — active edge of lesion; full-thickness skin biopsy (punch 4 mm).
  • Histopathology
    • TT — epithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells; nerve destruction; scanty/absent AFB; clear zone around nerves (perineural mononuclear infiltrate).
    • LL — diffuse infiltrate of foamy macrophages (Virchow cells) loaded with bacilli (globi); Grenz zone (subepidermal clear zone separating infiltrate from atrophic epidermis); numerous AFB.
    • BT/BB/BL — intermediate features.
  • Stains — H&E (granuloma pattern); Fite-Faraco or Wade-Fite (modified ZN) for AFB; S100 immunostain highlights damaged nerves.

4. Nerve Biopsy

  • Sural nerve biopsy — for pure neuritic leprosy (no skin lesions); diagnostic when skin smear/biopsy negative.
  • Shows endoneural granulomatous inflammation; nerve destruction; AFB.
  • Limit — causes sensory deficit in distribution of biopsied nerve.

5. Serology

  • Phenolic glycolipid-1 (PGL-1) antibody ELISA — detects IgM anti-PGL-1 (specific for M. leprae); sensitivity 95% in LL, 30% in TT; useful for diagnosis in multibacillary cases & epidemiological surveys.
  • ND-O-LID (natural disaccharide octyl glycoside linked to leprosy ID) — improved PGL-1 test.
  • Anti-LID-1 (leprosy ID-derived protein) — antibody & antigen detection; newer tests.
  • Serology is not used alone — clinical & smear remain mainstays.

6. Molecular Tests

  • PCR for M. leprae DNA — targets 16S rRNA, RLEP repeats, 854 bp repeat, folp1, rpoB; sensitivity 50–80%; specificity >95%; detects M. leprae in skin biopsy, nerve, nasal swab.
  • Real-time PCR — quantitative; useful for monitoring.
  • Drug resistance detection — PCR & sequencing for folp1 (dapsone), rpoB (rifampicin), gyrA (fluoroquinolone) mutations.
  • Nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) — not widely available in field.

7. Mouse Footpad Culture

  • Historical method; M. leprae can be cultivated in mouse footpad (cool temperature); takes 6–12 months.
  • Used for drug susceptibility testing; research only — not for clinical diagnosis.
  • Armadillo — alternative model (lower body temperature; supports high bacillary load).

8. Lepromin Test (Mitsuda reaction)

  • Intradermal injection of killed M. leprae suspension; read at 4 weeks (delayed hypersensitivity — granuloma formation, nodule).
  • Used to classify leprosy type & assess host immunity:
    • Strongly positive — TT (good prognosis).
    • Weak/negative — LL (poor prognosis).
    • Intermediate — borderline.
  • NOT diagnostic — also positive in BCG-vaccinated, healthy exposed individuals.
  • Now rarely used.

Treatment — Multidrug Therapy (MDT)

Type Drugs Duration
Paucibacillary (PB) — 1–5 lesions, smear-negativeRifampicin 600 mg monthly (supervised) + Dapsone 100 mg daily6 months
Multibacillary (MB) — >5 lesions, or smear-positiveRifampicin 600 mg + Clofazimine 300 mg monthly (supervised) + Dapsone 100 mg + Clofazimine 50 mg daily12 months
Single lesion PBSingle-dose ROM: Rifampicin 600 mg + Ofloxacin 400 mg + Minocycline 100 mgSingle dose

Prevention

  • Early detection & MDT — reduces transmission.
  • BCG vaccine — variable protection (20–80%; given for TB but cross-protects against leprosy).
  • Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) — single-dose rifampicin for contacts of newly diagnosed cases (LPEP programme).
  • Surveillance — active case finding in endemic areas; contact examination.
  • Rehabilitation — physiotherapy, ulcer care, surgery for deformity (claw hand, foot drop, lagophthalmos); protective footwear; psychological support.

Clinical Pearl

The single most reliable clinical sign of leprosy is anaesthetic skin lesion — test sensation with a wisp of cotton & pinprick; a hypopigmented or reddish patch that does not feel touch/pin = leprosy until proven otherwise. Skin smear from ear lobe & lesion edge (Ziehl-Neelsen stain) shows AFB in multibacillary cases; biopsy with Fite-Faraco stain confirms & classifies disease. PCR for M. leprae is useful for paucibacillary cases that are smear-negative. Always examine peripheral nerves — great auricular, ulnar, peroneal, posterior tibial — for thickening & tenderness; pure neuritic leprosy (no skin lesions) is common in India & requires nerve biopsy for diagnosis. Always look for & treat reactions aggressively — Type 1 (reversal) with steroids; Type 2 (ENL) with thalidomide (in males & post-menopausal women; strictly contraindicated in pregnancy — severe phocomelia) or steroids. Leprosy is curable — MDT kills M. leprae within days to weeks (rifampicin kills 99.9% with single dose); treatment is for fixed duration (6 months PB / 12 months MB) — not based on smear negativity. India eliminated leprosy as public health problem in 2005 (prevalence <1/10,000) but still has ~120,000 new cases annually — including child cases (indicating ongoing transmission). The hidden cases (untreated, marginalised) are the major challenge — particularly in Bihar, UP, Maharashtra, Odisha, Chhattisgarh.

Introduction

Staphylococcus aureus is one of the most successful human pathogens, causing infections ranging from minor skin abscesses to life-threatening endocarditis, osteomyelitis, and sepsis. Its remarkable virulence is due to a diverse array of cell-wall components, enzymes, toxins, and regulatory systems — many controlled by the agr (accessory gene regulator) quorum-sensing system.

1. Cell-Wall Associated Virulence Factors

1.1 Capsule

  • Polysaccharide microcapsule (type 5 & 8 — most common in clinical strains).
  • Anti-phagocytic — prevents opsonisation & complement activation.
  • Important in bacteraemia & endocarditis.

1.2 Protein A

  • Surface protein anchored to peptidoglycan.
  • Binds Fc portion of IgG in wrong orientation (Fc binding prevents opsonisation & phagocytosis).
  • Also a B-cell superantigen (protein A binds VH3 BCR → polyclonal B cell activation).
  • Major immune evasion mechanism.

1.3 Teichoic Acid & Lipoteichoic Acid

  • Cell-wall polymers; anchored to peptidoglycan (wall teichoic acid) or membrane (lipoteichoic acid).
  • Bind fibronectin — mediate adherence to mucosal surfaces, endothelium, and prosthetic devices (important in endocarditis & device infection).
  • Activate alternative complement; cytokine induction (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6).

1.4 Peptidoglycan

  • Endotoxin-like activity (despite being Gram-positive).
  • Activates alternative complement; cytokine induction; bone resorption (osteomyelitis).

1.5 Clumping Factor (Bound Coagulase)

  • Surface protein (ClfA, ClfB) that binds fibrinogen directly.
  • Converts fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin on bacterial surface → bacteria coated with fibrin → resists phagocytosis.
  • Slide coagulase test detects this factor.
  • Important in abscess formation & endocarditis (vegetation).

2. Extracellular Enzymes

2.1 Coagulase (Free)

  • Secreted enzyme that activates prothrombin → thrombin → converts fibrinogen to fibrin → clot formation.
  • Walls off infection → abscess formation; protects bacteria from phagocytes & antibiotics.
  • Tube coagulase test detects this factor.
  • Major virulence factor; definitive for S. aureus identification.

2.2 Catalase

  • Converts H₂O₂ → H₂O + O₂ (bubbles).
  • Protects from neutrophil oxidative killing (respiratory burst).
  • Distinguishes Staphylococcus (+) from Streptococcus (–).

2.3 Fibrinolysin (Staphylokinase)

  • Dissolves fibrin clots → aids spread through tissue.
  • Activates plasminogen → plasmin → fibrinolysis.

2.4 Hyaluronidase

  • Hydrolyses hyaluronic acid in connective tissue ground substance.
  • "Spreading factor" — facilitates tissue invasion.

2.5 DNase (Nuclease)

  • Degrades DNA in pus → reduces viscosity.
  • Aids spread through abscessed tissue.
  • Thermostable nuclease — heat-resistant (100 °C × 15 min); specific for S. aureus.

2.6 Lipase

  • Hydrolyses lipids & sebum.
  • Important in cutaneous infections (furuncles, carbuncles, wound infection) — S. aureus thrives in lipid-rich sebaceous glands.
  • Also hydrolyses lipids in food — contributes to food spoilage.

2.7 Phosphatase, Protease, Elastase, Collagenase

  • Tissue destruction; aid spread; contribute to necrosis.

2.8 β-Lactamase (Penicillinase)

  • Hydrolyses β-lactam ring → inactivates penicillin, ampicillin, piperacillin.
  • Plasmid-encoded (transmissible); ~90% of clinical strains produce.
  • Reason penicillin is no longer empirical therapy for S. aureus.

2.9 Penicillin-Binding Protein 2a (PBP2a, mecA gene)

  • Altered penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for β-lactam antibiotics.
  • Confers resistance to methicillin, oxacillin, nafcillin, all β-lactams (except ceftaroline).
  • Encoded by mecA gene on SCCmec (staphylococcal cassette chromosome mec) mobile genetic element.
  • Defines MRSA (methicillin-resistant S. aureus).

3. Cytolytic Toxins (Pore-Forming)

3.1 α-Haemolysin (α-Toxin)

  • Pore-forming toxin on RBC, WBC, platelets, endothelial cells, keratinocytes.
  • β-barrel pore → osmotic lysis, cell death.
  • Major dermonecrotic toxin — causes tissue necrosis in skin infections.
  • Causes haemolysis (β-haemolysis on blood agar); vascular injury; platelet aggregation.

3.2 β-Haemolysin (Sphingomyelinase)

  • Hydrolyses sphingomyelin in RBC membranes.
  • Cold-active ("hot-cold lysis" — incubate at 37 °C, then refrigerate at 4 °C → clear haemolysis).
  • Less important in humans; sheep RBC sensitive.

3.3 γ-Haemolysin & δ-Toxin

  • Bicomponent leucocidin; pore-forming on neutrophils, macrophages.
  • δ-toxin — detergent-like; lytic.

3.4 Panton-Valentine Leucocidin (PVL)

  • Bicomponent pore-forming toxin (LukS-PV + LukF-PV).
  • Destroys neutrophils & macrophages → release of inflammatory mediators → tissue necrosis.
  • Associated with community-associated MRSA (CA-MRSA) — USA300 clone.
  • Clinical associations:
    • Necrotising pneumonia (post-influenza; mortality 30–50%).
    • Recurrent skin & soft tissue abscesses.
    • Necrotising fasciitis.
  • Encoded by lukS-PV / lukF-PV genes (lysogenic phage).

3.5 Other Leucocidins

  • LukAB (LukGH) — targets neutrophils, macrophages; major in bloodstream infections.
  • LukED — targets CCR5+ cells (T cells, macrophages); role in severe infection.
  • γ-Haemolysin (HlgAB, HlgCB) — broad cell targets.

4. Superantigen Toxins

4.1 Toxic Shock Syndrome Toxin-1 (TSST-1)

  • 22 kDa protein; superantigen.
  • Binds MHC class II outside peptide groove + TCR Vβ2 → activates 5–30% of all T cells → massive cytokine release (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, IFN-γ) → cytokine storm.
  • Clinical — toxic shock syndrome (TSS): sudden high fever, hypotension, diffuse maculopapular rash (desquamates 1–2 weeks later, palms & soles), multi-organ failure (vomiting, diarrhoea, myalgia, conjunctivitis, renal, hepatic, haematological, CNS).
  • Menstrual TSS (super-absorbent tampon) & non-menstrual TSS (surgical wound, burn, postpartum).

4.2 Enterotoxins (A, B, C1, C2, C3, D, E, G–U)

  • Heat-stable (survive 100 °C × 30 min); resistant to digestive enzymes.
  • Superantigen activity (activate T cells via Vβ).
  • Act on intestinal epithelium & vagal afferents → vomiting.
  • Cause staphylococcal food poisoning — acute onset (1–6 h) of severe vomiting, abdominal cramps; diarrhoea less prominent; self-limited (24 h).
  • Source — contaminated food (cream pastries, mayonnaise, dairy, meats) left at room temperature.

4.3 Exfoliative Toxins A & B (ETA, ETB)

  • Serine proteases.
  • Cleave desmoglein 1 (Dsg1) — desmosomal cadherin in stratum granulosum → loss of keratinocyte adhesion → intraepidermal split.
  • Cause Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS)
    • Ritter's disease (neonatal generalised form).
    • Bullous impetigo (localised form).
    • Diffuse erythema, skin tenderness, large flaccid bullae, sheet-like desquamation; Nikolsky sign positive.
    • Toxin disseminates haematogenously from localised infection; mucosa spared (unlike TEN).
  • ETA — chromosomal; ETB — plasmid-encoded.

5. Other Virulence Factors

5.1 Biofilm Formation

  • Polysaccharide intercellular adhesin (PIA) — encoded by icaADBC operon.
  • Mediates adhesion to prosthetic materials (catheters, prosthetic joints, heart valves) and biofilm formation.
  • Biofilm protects from antibiotics (reduced penetration, metabolic dormancy) & immune attack.
  • Major cause of device-related infections (CRBSI, prosthetic joint infection, endocarditis on prosthetic valve).
  • PIA-independent biofilm — also via Aap (accumulation-associated protein), fibronectin-binding proteins.

5.2 Small-Colony Variants (SCVs)

  • Naturally occurring subpopulation; slow growth; small (<1/10 normal size) colonies.
  • Respiratory-deficient (mutations in electron transport chain — menadione/thymidine auxotrophs).
  • Persistent infections — chronic osteomyelitis, cystic fibrosis lung infection, device infection.
  • Resistant to aminoglycosides (reduced uptake), cell-wall antibiotics (slow growth); intracellular survival.

5.3 Arginine Catabolic Mobile Element (ACME)

  • Encoded by USA300 CA-MRSA (epidemic clone in USA).
  • Enhances colonisation (survival on skin); polyamine resistance; resistance to innate antimicrobial peptides.
  • Contributes to virulence of CA-MRSA.

5.4 Iron Acquisition Systems

  • Siderophores — staphyloferrin A, staphyloferrin B, aureochelin.
  • Staphylobactin — iron acquisition from heme.
  • Essential for survival in iron-limited host environment.

6. Regulatory Systems

  • agr (accessory gene regulator) — quorum-sensing system; activated at high cell density; upregulates toxins & enzymes (post-exponential phase); downregulates surface adhesins.
  • sarA (staphylococcal accessory regulator) — controls agr & other virulence genes.
  • SaeRS, ArlRS, SrrAB, LytSR — two-component regulatory systems.
  • Sigma factor B (σᴮ) — stress response; biofilm formation.
  • Coordinated regulation allows S. aureus to switch between colonisation (adhesion) & invasion (toxin production) phases.

Clinical Pearl

The coagulase test remains the single most important diagnostic test to differentiate S. aureus (positive) from coagulase-negative staphylococci. PVL-positive strains (especially USA300 CA-MRSA) cause necrotising pneumonia with 30–50% mortality — typically post-influenza; suspected in young healthy adults with rapidly progressive pneumonia, haemoptysis, leucopenia, and high fever. Treatment — vancomycin + linezolid + clindamycin (suppress toxin synthesis). TSST-1 — always consider toxic shock in any patient with fever, hypotension, diffuse rash, and multi-organ involvement — remove tampon/wound packing immediately; aggressive fluid resuscitation; IV antibiotics (clindamycin suppresses toxin; vancomycin/oxacillin for organism). SSSS in neonates — look for Nikolsky sign (skin peels with light stroking); mucous membranes spared (distinguishes from Stevens-Johnson/TEN); treat with anti-staphylococcal antibiotics (flucloxacillin/nafcillin) + supportive wound care. Biofilm on prosthetic devices — reason why device removal is often necessary for cure (antibiotics alone cannot eradicate biofilm); rifampin has biofilm activity (used in combination for prosthetic joint infection). SCVs are the cause of persistent infection — slow-growing, intracellular, antibiotic-tolerant; require prolonged therapy & often surgical source control.

Introduction

Diagnosis of leprosy is primarily clinical — based on cardinal signs defined by WHO. Laboratory tests confirm the diagnosis, classify the type, and assess bacterial load. Mycobacterium leprae cannot be cultured on artificial media, making diagnosis challenging.

WHO Cardinal Signs (Clinical Diagnosis)

Presence of ≥1 of the following confirms leprosy:

  1. Hypopigmented or reddish skin lesion with definite loss of sensation (test with cotton wisp & pinprick).
  2. Thickened peripheral nerves with loss of sensation in the area supplied (great auricular, ulnar, radial cutaneous, common peroneal, posterior tibial, sural).
  3. Skin smear positive for acid-fast bacilli (AFB).

Laboratory Tests

1. Skin Smear (Slit-Skin Smear) — Direct Evidence

  • Procedure:
    1. Pinch skin fold between thumb & forefinger (to make bloodless).
    2. Small incision (5 mm long, 3 mm deep) with sterile scalpel blade.
    3. Scrape dermal tissue with blade edge (turn blade 90°).
    4. Smear on clean slide; fix with heat.
    5. Stain with Ziehl-Neelsen or Fite-Faraco (modified ZN — uses weaker decolouriser as M. leprae is less acid-fast than M. tuberculosis).
  • Sites — 6 sites: both ear lobes, both eyebrows, edge of active lesion, and one normal-appearing skin (control). Ear lobes & eyebrows preferred (cooler temperature, high yield in LL).
  • Bacterial Index (BI) — Ridley's logarithmic scale (0–6+)
    • 0 — no bacilli in 100 oil-immersion fields.
    • 1+ — 1–10 bacilli per 100 fields.
    • 2+ — 1–10 bacilli per 10 fields.
    • 3+ — 1–10 bacilli per field.
    • 4+ — 10–100 bacilli per field.
    • 5+ — 100–1000 bacilli per field.
    • 6+ — >1000 bacilli per field (globi — clusters of bacilli in macrophages; pathognomonic of LL).
  • Morphological Index (MI) — percentage of solid-staining (live) bacilli vs fragmented (dead); monitors treatment response (MI falls rapidly with effective MDT).
  • Sensitivity — high in LL, BL (multibacillary); low in TT, BT, indeterminate (paucibacillary — usually negative).
  • Limitation — insensitive for PB leprosy; cannot diagnose TT (smear-negative).

2. Skin Biopsy — Histopathology

  • Site — active edge of lesion (most inflamed border); full-thickness punch biopsy (4 mm) including subcutaneous fat.
  • Stains:
    • H&E — assess granuloma pattern & morphology.
    • Fite-Faraco or Wade-Fite (modified ZN) — AFB stain; M. leprae appears red.
    • S100 immunostain — highlights Schwann cells & damaged nerves.
    • CD1a, CD68 — immune phenotyping.
  • Histology by type:
    Type Histology
    TTEpithelioid granulomas with Langhans giant cells; perineural mononuclear infiltrate ("onion-skin"); nerve destruction; scanty/absent AFB; epidermis atrophic; clear Grenz zone absent
    BTEpithelioid granulomas; some Schwann cell destruction; scanty AFB
    BBMixed; epithelioid + macrophage granulomas; moderate AFB
    BLFoamy macrophages; some epithelioid cells; many AFB; Grenz zone present
    LLDiffuse infiltrate of foamy macrophages (Virchow cells) loaded with bacilli (globi); Grenz zone (subepidermal clear zone); epidermis atrophic; numerous AFB; plasma cells & lymphocytes
    IndeterminateNon-specific mild lymphocytic infiltrate around nerves & vessels; AFB usually absent

3. Nerve Biopsy

  • Sural nerve biopsy — for pure neuritic leprosy (no skin lesions); also when skin smear/biopsy are inconclusive.
  • Shows endoneural granulomatous inflammation; nerve destruction; AFB in Schwann cells.
  • Skin biopsy is preferred first — nerve biopsy causes sensory deficit in distribution of biopsied nerve (lateral foot for sural).
  • Other nerves — superficial radial, superficial peroneal (rare).

4. Serology

  • Phenolic glycolipid-1 (PGL-1) antibody ELISA
    • Detects IgM antibodies to PGL-1 (specific to M. leprae).
    • Sensitivity — 95% in LL; 30–40% in TT; 60% in borderline.
    • Specificity — 90–95%; cross-reactivity with M. tuberculosis, BCG.
    • Useful for confirmation in multibacillary cases & epidemiological surveys.
    • Not used alone — false negatives in PB leprosy.
  • ND-O-BSA (natural disaccharide octyl bovine serum albumin) — improved PGL-1 antigen; better sensitivity.
  • LID-1 (leprosy ID-derived protein) — antibody & antigen detection; newer tests.
  • Anti-phenolic glycolipid-I (PGL-I) IgM — declines with treatment; useful for monitoring.
  • NFC (Nerve Function Test — Nerve Conduction Study) — for asymptomatic nerve damage; detects subclinical neuropathy in contacts.

5. Molecular Tests — PCR

  • PCR targets — RLEP repeats (most sensitive), 16S rRNA, 854 bp repeat, folp1, rpoB, pra (Lsr2), Ag85B.
  • Sensitivity — 50–80% (varies by sample type & load); higher in multibacillary.
  • Specificity — >95%; distinguishes M. leprae from other mycobacteria.
  • Specimens — skin biopsy, slit-skin smear, nerve biopsy, nasal swab.
  • Real-time PCR — quantitative; useful for monitoring treatment response.
  • Drug resistance detection:
    • folp1 mutations — dihydropteroate synthase — dapsone resistance.
    • rpoB mutations — RNA polymerase β-subunit — rifampicin resistance.
    • gyrA mutations — DNA gyrase — fluoroquinolone resistance.
  • Limitation — PCR detects DNA from live & dead bacilli; positive PCR after treatment does not indicate active disease.
  • Not widely available in field settings.

6. Lepromin Test (Mitsuda Reaction)

  • Procedure — intradermal injection of killed M. leprae suspension (lepromin) into forearm; read reaction at 4 weeks (late / Mitsuda reaction).
  • Interpretation:
    • Strongly positive (≥5 mm nodule, may ulcerate) — TT (good prognosis; strong cell-mediated immunity).
    • Negative (<3 mm) — LL (poor prognosis; absent CMI).
    • Intermediate (3–5 mm) — borderline leprosy.
  • Purpose — classify type of leprosy & assess host immunity; helps predict prognosis & risk of reactions.
  • NOT diagnostic — positive in BCG-vaccinated, healthy exposed individuals, tuberculoid leprosy; negative in LL but also in some healthy individuals.
  • Also read early reaction (Fernandez) at 24–48 h — DTH to soluble antigens.
  • Now rarely used in clinical practice.

7. Mouse Footpad Culture

  • Historical; M. leprae multiplies in mouse footpad (cooler temperature, 30–32 °C) over 6–12 months.
  • Used for:
    • Confirming viability of bacilli.
    • Drug susceptibility testing (dapsone, rifampicin, clofazimine).
    • Research — vaccine development, pathogenesis.
  • Armadillo — alternative model (low body temperature; supports high bacillary load; used for antigen production).
  • Not available for clinical diagnosis — too slow.

8. Other Tests

  • Slit-skin smear from nasal mucosa — for nasal carriage in LL; high bacillary load.
  • Nerve conduction studies (NCS) — detect subclinical neuropathy; monitor nerve function during treatment & reactions.
  • Warm immersion test / cold test — assess sensory loss.
  • Ultrasound of peripheral nerves — thickening, echotexture changes; non-invasive.
  • Photography & body chart — document lesions for monitoring.

Diagnostic Algorithm

  1. Clinical examination — skin lesion + sensory loss + nerve thickening → diagnose.
  2. Skin smear — for confirmation & classification (PB vs MB).
  3. Skin biopsy — for histopathological classification; when smear negative (PB leprosy); pure neuritic leprosy (nerve biopsy).
  4. PCR — if available, for confirmation in difficult cases (PB, pure neuritic, paediatric).
  5. Serology (PGL-1) — for epidemiological surveys; not for routine clinical diagnosis.
  6. Lepromin test — optional; for classification & prognosis.

Treatment Classification Based on Diagnosis

Classification MDT regimen Duration
Paucibacillary (PB) — 1–5 lesions; smear-negativeRifampicin 600 mg monthly + Dapsone 100 mg daily6 months
Multibacillary (MB) — >5 lesions or smear-positiveRifampicin 600 mg + Clofazimine 300 mg monthly + Dapsone 100 mg + Clofazimine 50 mg daily12 months
Single lesion PBROM: Rifampicin 600 mg + Ofloxacin 400 mg + Minocycline 100 mg single doseSingle dose

Clinical Pearl

The single most reliable clinical sign of leprosy is anaesthetic skin lesion — test sensation with wisp of cotton & pinprick. Skin smear from ear lobe & lesion edge (ZN or Fite-Faraco) shows AFB in multibacillary (LL, BL) cases; biopsy with Fite-Faraco stain confirms & classifies disease even in paucibacillary (smear-negative) cases. PCR for M. leprae (RLEP target) is the most sensitive test for paucibacillary & pure neuritic leprosy but not widely available. Always examine peripheral nerves — pure neuritic leprosy (no skin lesions) accounts for 5–10% of cases in India & requires nerve biopsy. Monitor treatment response with BI (falls 1 log per year with MDT) & MI (falls rapidly within weeks); persistent high MI suggests dapsone resistance (check folp1 PCR). Serology (PGL-1 IgM) is useful for epidemiological surveys — detects subclinical infection in contacts; seropositive contacts have higher risk of developing disease. Lepromin test is now obsolete — used historically for classification. Always look for & treat reactions (Type 1 reversal & Type 2 ENL) — these can cause irreversible nerve damage if untreated.

Introduction

Parvovirus B19 — a small (18–26 nm), non-enveloped, single-stranded DNA virus of family Parvoviridae, genus Erythroparvovirus — is the only parvovirus known to cause human disease. Discovered in 1975 (Cossart, while screening blood donors for hepatitis B). Target cell: erythroid progenitor cells (P-antigen / globoside receptor in bone marrow); causes transient red cell aplasia.

Transmission

  • Respiratory droplets — primary route (cough, sneeze; "fifth disease" in children).
  • Vertical (transplacental) — pregnant woman to fetus; risk of hydrops fetalis & fetal loss (especially 2nd trimester).
  • Blood products — Factor VIII/IX concentrates (heat-resistant virus); pooled plasma.
  • Organ transplantation — rare.
  • Incubation — 4–21 days (usually 7–10); infectivity highest before rash appears (viraemic phase).
  • Seroprevalence — 50% by age 15, 80% by age 40; lifelong immunity.

Clinical Manifestations

1. Erythema Infectiosum (Fifth Disease)

  • Most common manifestation in children.
  • Stage 1 — prodrome: mild fever, malaise, headache, sore throat (non-specific).
  • Stage 2 — "slapped-cheek" rash: bright erythema on both cheeks (spares nasal bridge & perioral area); circumoral pallor; 1–4 days.
  • Stage 3 — body rash: maculopapular erythematous rash on trunk & extensor surfaces of limbs → reticular/lace-like pattern (central clearing); lasts 1–3 weeks; may fluctuate with heat, sunlight, exercise, stress.
  • Mild fever; arthralgia in adults.
  • Self-limiting in 1–2 weeks.

2. Arthropathy / Arthritis

  • More common in adults (especially women); ~60% of adult women.
  • Symmetric, small-joint arthritis (hands, wrists, knees, ankles); resembles rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Lasts 1–3 weeks; usually resolves without sequelae; may persist or recur for months.
  • May mimic juvenile idiopathic arthritis in children.
  • Rheumatoid factor may be transiently positive.

3. Transient Aplastic Crisis (TAC)

  • Occurs in patients with underlying haemolytic anaemia — sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis, thalassaemia, G6PD deficiency, pyruvate kinase deficiency.
  • Parvovirus infects & destroys erythroid progenitors (P-antigen / globoside receptor on erythroblasts) → abrupt cessation of erythropoiesis → precipitous fall in haemoglobin (reticulocytopenia).
  • Sudden severe anaemia — pallor, fatigue, dyspnoea, heart failure; may be life-threatening.
  • Self-limiting (7–10 days) once neutralising antibody develops; reticulocytes reappear → recovery.
  • Does not cause chronic infection in immunocompetent (IgG clears virus).

4. Pure Red Cell Aplasia (PRCA) in Immunocompromised

  • In immunodeficient patients (HIV/AIDS, leukaemia, transplant recipients, congenital immunodeficiency) — cannot mount neutralising antibody response → persistent parvovirus infection → chronic red cell aplasia.
  • Severe chronic anaemia; reticulocytopenia; requires IVIG (provides neutralising antibody).
  • May relapse — repeated IVIG courses.

5. Hydrops Fetalis & Congenital Infection

  • Vertical transmission rate — 30% (maternal infection during pregnancy).
  • Risk highest in 1st & 2nd trimester (10–12 weeks).
  • Fetal infection → destruction of erythroid progenitors → severe anaemia → high-output cardiac failure → hydrops fetalis (ascites, pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, subcutaneous oedema); may resolve spontaneously or progress to fetal death (2–6% risk).
  • Maternal infection during pregnancy — fetal loss rate ~10% (highest in 2nd trimester; rare congenital anomalies).
  • Diagnosis — fetal anaemia on Doppler (middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity >1.5 MoM); PCR of amniotic fluid; fetal blood sampling.
  • Treatment — intrauterine blood transfusion for severe fetal anaemia; can be life-saving.
  • Parvovirus is the most common infectious cause of non-immune hydrops fetalis.

6. Other Manifestations

  • Papular-purpuric gloves-and-socks syndrome (PPGSS) — painful erythema & petechiae on hands & feet; young adults; self-limiting.
  • Myocarditis & dilated cardiomyopathy — rare.
  • Glomerulonephritis, vasculitis, Henoch-Schönlein purpura — immune complex mediated.
  • Neurologic — encephalitis, meningitis, stroke, peripheral neuropathy, brachial plexus neuropathy.
  • Hepatitis — mild transaminitis; rare fulminant.
  • Masked infection — reactivation in immunosuppressed or pregnancy.

Pathogenesis

  1. Entry — respiratory route → viraemia (day 5–10).
  2. Receptor — globoside (P antigen / Gb4) on erythroid progenitors in bone marrow; also on megakaryocytes, endothelial cells, placenta, fetal liver, heart.
  3. Erythroid aplasia — viral non-structural protein NS1 induces apoptosis of erythroblasts → arrest at colony-forming unit (CFU-E) stage.
  4. Immune complex formation — IgM & IgG antibodies → circulating immune complexes deposited in skin & joints → rash & arthritis (coincides with appearance of antibody).
  5. Viraemia clears within 1–2 weeks with IgG response; patient no longer infectious once rash appears.

Laboratory Diagnosis

  • Serology
    • IgM anti-parvovirus B19 — appears day 10–14; persists 3–6 months; indicates acute/recent infection.
    • IgG anti-parvovirus B19 — appears day 14–21; persists for life; indicates past infection (immunity).
    • Methods — ELISA, chemiluminescence, immunofluorescence.
  • PCR (DNA)
    • Detects viral DNA in serum, bone marrow, amniotic fluid, fetal blood, tissue.
    • Most sensitive — especially in immunocompromised (no antibody response) & fetus.
    • Quantitative — for monitoring.
  • Bone marrow biopsy
    • Shows giant proerythroblasts (pathognomonic) with viral inclusions; absence of mature erythroid cells; myeloid & megakaryocytic series preserved.
  • CBC
    • Normocytic normochromic anaemia; reticulocytopenia (<0.5%) — hallmark of aplastic crisis; leukopenia, thrombocytopenia may occur.
  • Fetal assessment — Doppler ultrasound (MCA-PSV for anaemia); amniocentesis for PCR; cordocentesis for fetal Hb.
  • Histopathology — giant proerythroblasts with viral inclusions in placenta, fetal liver, bone marrow.

Treatment

  • Healthy children & adults — symptomatic (NSAIDs for arthralgia); self-limiting.
  • Aplastic crisis — blood transfusion until reticulocytes reappear; isolate patient (infectious); oxygen support.
  • Immunocompromised / PRCA — IVIG 400 mg/kg/day × 5–10 days (provides neutralising antibody); may need repeated courses; reduce immunosuppression if possible.
  • Hydrops fetalis — intrauterine blood transfusion through cordocentesis; may repeat; delivery if viable.
  • Pregnancy — counsel; serial ultrasound; monitor fetal anaemia; no antiviral specifically approved.

Prevention

  • No vaccine widely available; candidates in clinical trials.
  • Infection control — droplet precautions in hospitalised patients with aplastic crisis (infectious before rash); standard precautions for fifth disease (not infectious once rash appears).
  • Pregnant healthcare workers — should avoid contact with patients in aplastic crisis; serological screening in pregnancy.
  • Blood product screening — for pooled plasma; heat-resistant virus survives standard pasteurisation.

Clinical Pearl

Parvovirus B19 should be suspected in any patient with sudden severe anaemia & reticulocytopenia, especially those with underlying haemolytic anaemia (sickle cell — "aplastic crisis"). The classic presentation in children is the "slapped cheek" rash of fifth disease — but the child is no longer infectious once the rash appears (viraemia precedes rash). In pregnant women exposed to parvovirus, check IgM & IgG — if IgM positive, monitor fetus with serial ultrasound for anaemia (MCA Doppler) for 8–12 weeks; intrauterine transfusion is life-saving for severe hydrops. Immunocompromised patients with chronic anaemia (HIV, transplant) — suspect persistent parvovirus infection (no antibody); diagnosis by PCR; treat with IVIG which provides exogenous neutralising antibody. The bone marrow finding of giant proerythroblasts is pathognomonic — large basophilic cells with viral inclusions, in an otherwise hypocellular erythroid series. Parvovirus is the most common infectious cause of non-immune hydrops fetalis — always check maternal parvovirus IgM in any pregnant woman with fetus showing hydrops. Note: the virus is heat-resistant — survives pasteurisation (56 °C × 60 min) and dry heat (80 °C × 72 h); reason for screening plasma pools by PCR.

Definition

Cutaneous larva migrans (CLM) — also called "creeping eruption", "ground itch", "sandworm disease", "plumber's itch" — is a parasitic skin disease caused by hookworm larvae of dogs & cats (animal hookworms) that penetrate human skin but cannot complete their life cycle, wandering aimlessly in the epidermis, producing characteristic serpiginous, intensely pruritic rash.

Etiology

  • Ancylostoma braziliense (most common — dog & cat hookworm).
  • Ancylostoma caninum (dog hookworm).
  • Ancylostoma ceylanicum (dog/cat hookworm — can mature in humans).
  • Uncinaria stenocephala (dog hookworm — Europe).
  • Bunostomum phlebotomum (cattle hookworm).
  • Strongyloides stercoralis (larva currens — rapid linear movement, not true CLM).
  • Gnathostoma spinigerum, Spirometra (sparganosis), Dirofilaria — less common.

Life Cycle & Pathogenesis

  1. Eggs shed in dog/cat faeces → contaminate soil (sandy beaches, moist shaded soil, under houses).
  2. Eggs hatch into rhabditiform larvae (non-infective) → moult into filariform (L3) larvae (infective) in 5–7 days.
  3. Human skin contact — larvae penetrate exposed skin (feet, buttocks, thighs, hands) through hair follicles or tiny abrasions.
  4. Migration — larvae shed their sheath, enter epidermis; cannot penetrate basement membrane (humans are abnormal hosts) → wander in stratum spinosum & granulosum for weeks to months, advancing 2–7 mm/day.
  5. Inflammatory response — eosinophils, lymphocytes, histiocytes around larvae → intensely pruritic erythematous serpiginous track.
  6. Larvae eventually die (unable to mature); no systemic infection (no pulmonary migration in CLM, unlike human hookworm).

Epidemiology

  • Most common in tropical & subtropical regions — Southeast Asia, Caribbean, Africa, South America, southeastern USA.
  • Associated with beaches, sandboxes, soil under houses where dogs/cats defecate.
  • Risk groups — beachgoers, sunbathers, children playing in sand, plumbers/electricians working under houses, gardeners, farmers, military personnel.
  • Travel history — "beach holiday with itchy rash on feet" is the classic story.

Clinical Features

  • Incubation — penetration often unnoticed; itching begins within hours.
  • Initial lesion — pruritic erythematous papule at site of penetration (feet in 70% of cases; buttocks, thighs, hands).
  • Classic feature — serpiginous, tortuous, erythematous, slightly raised track 2–3 mm wide; advances 2–7 mm per day; intensely pruritic.
  • Track may extend several cm; multiple tracks if multiple larvae.
  • Scratching → excoriation, secondary bacterial infection (S. aureus, Streptococcus), regional lymphadenitis.
  • Vesicobullous lesions may form along track (especially soles).
  • Without treatment — lesions persist for weeks to months (larvae may live 6–12 months in skin); eventually die & resolve.
  • Systemic symptoms absent (no eosinophilia usually; no pulmonary phase).

Differential Diagnosis

Condition Distinguishing feature
Larva currens (Strongyloides)Rapid migration (~5–10 cm/hour, vs 2–7 mm/day in CLM); perianal/buttock location; recurrent; associated with Strongyloides hyperinfection; eosinophilia
Migrating botfly larva (Dermatobia hominis)Central punctum with larva; furuncle-like nodule; not serpiginous
ScabiesBurrows in finger webs, wrists, genitalia; mite visible in burrow
Tinea corporisAnnular lesion with central clearing; stationary; KOH positive
Contact dermatitisVesicular, linear, history of plant/contact exposure; not migratory
Erythema migrans (Lyme disease)Slowly expanding annular lesion with central clearing (target); tick bite history; Borrelia burgdorferi
Sparganosis (Spirometra)Subcutaneous nodule; migratory; history of applying frog/fish flesh to skin
GnathostomiasisMigratory subcutaneous swelling; eosinophilia; Southeast Asia; raw fish

Laboratory Diagnosis

  • Primarily clinical — history (travel, beach exposure, pets) + characteristic serpiginous rash.
  • Skin biopsy — rarely needed; may show larva in epidermis with surrounding eosinophilic infiltrate (but larvae are ahead of visible track, so biopsy often misses).
  • CBC — eosinophilia uncommon (larvae stay in skin; no systemic phase); if high eosinophilia, consider Strongyloides.
  • Serology — not useful for animal hookworms.
  • Dermoscopy — may reveal larval tract; not routinely used.

Treatment

  • Drug of choice — oral albendazole 400 mg daily × 3–7 days OR ivermectin 200 µg/kg single dose (or repeat at 7 days).
  • Mebendazole 100 mg BD × 3 days — alternative.
  • Topical thiabendazole 10–15% suspension/cream applied BID × 5–7 days — for early/localised lesions; less effective than oral.
  • Topical ivermectin 1% — emerging option.
  • Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen — freezing the leading edge of the track; painful, may require multiple sessions; less effective than oral therapy; risk of ulceration.
  • Antihistamines — for pruritus.
  • Antibiotics — for secondary bacterial infection (dicloxacillin, cephalexin).
  • Most cases resolve within 1–2 weeks of treatment.

Prevention

  • Avoid walking barefoot on beaches/sandy soil where dogs/cats defecate.
  • Wear shoes/sandals on beaches, especially in tropics.
  • Use beach mats/towels rather than lying directly on sand.
  • De-worm pets regularly (dogs & cats).
  • Control stray animal populations on beaches.
  • Avoid sandy areas visible with animal faeces; cover sandboxes when not in use.
  • Travel health education — sunbathers should lie on towels, not bare sand.

Clinical Pearl

The single most important clinical clue is the serpiginous, creeping rash that advances a few mm per day, intensely pruritic, on the foot of a beachgoer. The larva is located at the leading edge of the visible track (a few mm ahead) — which is why biopsies often miss and why topical therapy applied to the entire track (especially the leading edge) is needed. Distinguish from larva currens (Strongyloides) — that moves much faster (5–10 cm/hour, vs 2–7 mm/day for CLM), often perianal/buttock location, and is associated with eosinophilia & pulmonary symptoms (Loeffler syndrome) due to systemic migration. Treatment of choice is oral ivermectin or albendazole — topical thiabendazole is painful, messy, and less effective. Cryotherapy alone is often ineffective because the larva is ahead of the visible track. Always warn patients about secondary infection from scratching — S. aureus cellulitis can complicate untreated lesions. For travellers — preventive advice is more effective than post-exposure treatment; the "beach barefoot" habit in tropical destinations is the leading risk.

Introduction

Syphilis is a chronic systemic sexually transmitted infection caused by Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum — a thin (0.1 × 5–20 µm), coiled (6–14 spirals), delicate, motile spirochete that cannot be cultured on artificial media. Untreated, syphilis progresses through characteristic stages — primary, secondary, latent, and tertiary — each with distinct clinical features.

Stages of Syphilis

1. Primary Syphilis

  • Incubation — 9–90 days (average 3 weeks) after sexual exposure.
  • Chancre — at site of inoculation (genital — glans penis, prepuce, vulva, cervix, labia; extragenital — lip, tongue, tonsil, anus, rectum, finger).
    • Single, painless, clean, indurated ulcer with raised edge ("cartilaginous" induration); 1–2 cm diameter; base clean, red, exudes clear serum.
    • Painless (distinguishes from herpes — painful; chancroid — painful; LGV — painful).
    • Regional lymphadenopathy — non-tender, rubbery, discrete, non-suppurating inguinal nodes ("satellite bubo"); bilateral.
    • Heals spontaneously in 3–6 weeks without scarring (even without treatment).
    • Does NOT bleed on touch (distinguishes from diphtheria pseudomembrane).
    • Extragenital chances are more atypical.
  • Highly infectious — teeming with spirochaetes; dark-field microscopy positive.
  • Serology may be negative in early primary (window period); becomes positive after 1–4 weeks.

2. Secondary Syphilis

  • Onset — 2 weeks to 6 months after primary chancre (average 6 weeks); may overlap with healing chancre.
  • Represents haematogenous dissemination of spirochaetes.
  • Constitutional — low-grade fever, malaise, fatigue, headache, anorexia, weight loss, generalised lymphadenopathy (epitrochlear node pathognomonic), arthralgia, myalgia.
  • Skin rash:
    • Macular / maculopapular rash on trunk, palms, soles, extremities; copper-red; non-pruritic (or mildly pruritic); symmetric; 5–10 mm.
    • Rash on palms & soles is highly suggestive of secondary syphilis (distinguishes from most other rashes).
    • Annular papular rash — face (especially black patients).
    • Condylomata lata — broad, moist, wart-like, highly infectious plaques in moist intertriginous areas (perianal, vulva, scrotum, inner thigh, axilla, submammary).
    • Patchy hair loss (moth-eaten alopecia) — eyebrows, beard, scalp; non-scarring.
    • Mucous patches — painless silver-grey erosions on tongue, buccal mucosa, lips, pharynx, genitalia; highly infectious.
  • Systemic manifestations:
    • Hepatitis (mild transaminitis); perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome).
    • Glomerulonephritis, nephrotic syndrome (immune complex).
    • Uveitis, optic neuritis, retinitis.
    • Meningitis, cranial nerve palsies (VII, VIII — sensorineural hearing loss), stroke.
    • Osteitis, periostitis, arthritis.
    • Malaise, fever, generalised lymphadenopathy (epitrochlear, inguinal, cervical).
  • Resolves spontaneously in 3–12 weeks → latent syphilis.
  • Highest spirochaete load → highly infectious.

3. Latent Syphilis

  • Asymptomatic phase after resolution of secondary syphilis; diagnosis by positive serology with no clinical signs.
  • Early latent — <1 year after infection (or unknown, but within last year); infectious (relapse possible).
  • Late latent — >1 year after infection (or unknown duration); not infectious (except transplacentally); can still transmit to fetus.
  • Can last for years to decades before progressing to tertiary.
  • ~30% progress to tertiary syphilis if untreated.

4. Tertiary (Late) Syphilis

Occurs in ~30% of untreated patients, 3–30 years after primary infection. Three main forms:

4a. Gummatous Syphilis (Late Benign Syphilis)

  • Gumma — granulomatous lesion with central caseous necrosis surrounded by plasma cells, lymphocytes, epithelioid cells, giant cells; paucibacillary (few or no treponemes); destructive but localised.
  • Skin — nodular ulcerative lesions with punched-out edges, scarring ("tissue paper" scars); annular pattern.
  • Mucous membranes — palate perforation (cleft palate); nasal septum perforation (saddle nose).
  • Bones — periostitis, osteitis (tibia, skull, clavicle); Charcot joints (neuropathic).
  • Viscera — gumma of liver (hepar lobatum), testis, stomach, lung, brain.
  • Responds dramatically to penicillin.

4b. Cardiovascular Syphilis

  • Occurs 10–30 years after primary infection.
  • Aortitis — infection of vasa vasorum of aorta → ischaemic necrosis of aortic media → aneurysm of ascending aorta & arch.
  • Clinical:
    • Aortic regurgitation — dilatation of aortic root & valve ring; diastolic murmur; water-hammer pulse; collapsing pulse; de Musset's sign (head bobbing); Corrigan's sign (visible carotid pulsation); Quincke's pulse (nail bed pulsation).
    • Aortic aneurysm — expanding mass in mediastinum; pressure on trachea (stridor), oesophagus (dysphagia), recurrent laryngeal nerve (hoarseness); risk of rupture.
    • Coronary ostial stenosis — angina.
    • Syphilitic aortitis — "tree-bark" appearance of intima (atherosclerosis-like).
  • Often asymptomatic until complications; leading cause of death in tertiary syphilis.

4c. Neurosyphilis

Can occur at any stage but typically tertiary. Four main forms:

  • Asymptomatic neurosyphilis — CSF abnormalities (pleocytosis, raised protein, positive CSF VDRL) without symptoms.
  • Meningovascular syphilis — 5–10 years after primary; chronic basal meningitis, vasculitis of cerebral vessels → stroke (especially middle cerebral artery); cranial nerve palsies (VII, VIII); seizures; headache.
  • General paresis (General Paralysis of the Insane — GPI) — 15–20 years after primary; direct parenchymal invasion of brain.
    • Psychiatric — personality change, dementia, delusions of grandeur, mania, depression, psychosis ("general paresis of the insane").
    • Neurological — Argyll Robertson pupils (small, irregular, accommodate but do not react to light — "prostitute's pupil"); tremor of tongue & hands (flapping); dysarthria; hyperreflexia; seizures; Babinski sign.
    • Progressive dementia & death within 3–5 years if untreated.
  • Tabes dorsalis (Locomotor ataxia) — 15–30 years after primary; degeneration of posterior columns & dorsal roots of spinal cord.
    • Sensory ataxia — wide-based gait, positive Romberg, foot slap; loss of position & vibration sense; loss of deep tendon reflexes (especially knee & ankle).
    • Lightning pains — sudden, severe, lancinating pains in legs, abdomen, throat.
    • Visceral crises — abdominal pain, vomiting (gastric crisis); rectal pain (rectal crisis); laryngeal stridor.
    • Charcot joints — neuropathic arthropathy (knee, hip, ankle); painless joint destruction.
    • Argyll Robertson pupil — accommodation present, light reflex absent.
    • Bladder & bowel dysfunction — urinary retention, constipation; trophic ulcers (perforating ulcers of foot).
    • Optic atrophy — blindness.

5. Congenital Syphilis

Transplacental transmission from mother to fetus — can occur at any stage of pregnancy but highest risk in primary & secondary maternal syphilis.

  • Early congenital syphilis (0–2 years):
    • "Snuffles" — profuse blood-tinged nasal discharge (highly infectious).
    • Maculopapular rash — palms, soles, perioral, perianal; desquamation.
    • Hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, anaemia, thrombocytopenia.
    • Osteochondritis & periostitis (Parrot's pseudoparalysis — infant does not move limb due to pain).
    • Lymphadenopathy.
    • Low birth weight, failure to thrive.
  • Late congenital syphilis (>2 years):
    • Hutchinson's triad: (1) Hutchinson's teeth — notched, peg-shaped permanent central incisors; (2) interstitial keratitis — bilateral corneal inflammation → opacity, blindness; (3) eighth nerve deafness (sensorineural, late onset).
    • Mulberry molars — multiple small cusps on first molars.
    • Saddle nose deformity, frontal bossing (Parrot's nodes), short maxilla, high arched palate, protuberant mandible ("bulldog" facies).
    • Saber shins (anterior bowing of tibia), scaphoid scapula, Clutton joints (painless knee effusion).
    • Rhagades — linear scars radiating from angles of mouth, nose, anus.
    • Mental retardation, seizures.

Laboratory Diagnosis

  • Direct detection
    • Dark-field microscopy — exudate from chancre, condyloma latum, mucous patch, snuffles → characteristic corkscrew motility.
    • DFA-TP (direct fluorescent antibody) — more sensitive & specific.
    • PCR — research; detects T. pallidum DNA.
  • Non-treponemal serology (reagin tests) — detect anti-lipoidal antibodies (reagin) produced in response to lipoidal antigens released from damaged tissues & T. pallidum cell wall.
    • VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) — flocculation test; quantitative (titre); screening.
    • RPR (Rapid Plasma Reagin) — similar to VDRL; macroscopic flocculation; faster.
    • USR (Unheated Serum Reagin), TRUST.
    • Titres correlate with disease activity — used to monitor treatment response (4-fold fall in titre at 6 months indicates adequate therapy).
    • False positive — pregnancy, autoimmune disease (SLE), malaria, leprosy, HIV, vaccination, IV drug use, old age.
    • False negative — prozone phenomenon (high antibody titre in secondary syphilis → false negative; dilute serum & retest).
  • Treponemal serology (specific tests) — detect antibodies against T. pallidum antigens.
    • FTA-ABS (Fluorescent Treponemal Antibody Absorption) — indirect immunofluorescence; sensitive & specific.
    • TPHA (T. pallidum Haemagglutination Assay) — passive haemagglutination.
    • TPPA (T. pallidum Particle Agglutination) — gelatin particle agglutination.
    • Western blot — confirms.
    • Rapid point-of-care treponemal tests — immunochromatographic; useful in field & screening.
    • EIA (enzyme immunoassay) — detects IgG, IgM; used for screening in many labs now.
  • Diagnostic algorithm:
    • Screen with VDRL/RPR → if positive, confirm with TPHA/FTA-ABS (treponemal test).
    • "Reverse algorithm": screen with EIA (treponemal) → if positive, do RPR (non-treponemal) for disease activity.
  • CSF examination — for suspected neurosyphilis: CSF VDRL (specific but insensitive), CSF protein, cells (lymphocytic pleocytosis), CSF FTA-ABS (sensitive but less specific).

Treatment

  • Drug of choice — Penicillin G (only antibiotic with proven efficacy for syphilis, especially neurosyphilis & pregnancy).
    • Primary, secondary, early latent — Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose.
    • Late latent, gumma, cardiovascular — Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM weekly × 3 doses.
    • Neurosyphilis — IV Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18–24 million units/day (3–4 MU every 4 h) × 10–14 days.
    • Congenital syphilis — IV or IM aqueous crystalline penicillin G 50,000 U/kg every 12 h × 10 days.
  • Penicillin allergy (non-pregnant):
    • Doxycycline 100 mg BD × 14 days (early syphilis).
    • Tetracycline 500 mg QID × 14 days.
    • Ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV/IM daily × 8–10 days (early syphilis; cross-reactivity with penicillin, test dose).
    • Azithromycin 2 g single dose — resistance reported (macrolide resistance — 23S rRNA mutation A2058G).
    • For late syphilis — doxycycline × 28 days.
  • Pregnancy — penicillin is the only option; desensitise if allergic.
  • Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction
    • Acute worsening of symptoms within 2–12 h of treatment (fever, chills, myalgia, headache, hypotension); due to massive release of lipopolysaccharide-like endotoxin from killed spirochaetes.
    • Most common in secondary syphilis.
    • Self-limiting (24 h); treat with antipyretics, fluids.
    • Risk in pregnancy — fetal distress, preterm labour; monitor.

Prevention

  • Safe sexual practices — condoms, mutual monogamy.
  • Screening — pregnant women (first antenatal visit, repeat in 3rd trimester if high risk); MSM; HIV-positive; sexual contacts of infected individuals.
  • Notification & treatment of partners — primary (3 months), secondary (6 months), latent (1 year).
  • Education — importance of completing treatment; follow-up serology.

Clinical Pearl

The single most important clinical clue to secondary syphilis is a painless rash on the palms & soles — few other conditions cause palmar-plantar rashes ( Rocky Mountain spotted fever, meningococcaemia, hand-foot-mouth disease, Kawasaki). Hutchinson's triad (Hutchinson's teeth, interstitial keratitis, 8th nerve deafness) is pathognomonic of late congenital syphilis. Argyll Robertson pupil (accommodates but does not react to light — "prostitute's pupil: accommodates but does not react") is classic for neurosyphilis (tabes dorsalis & general paresis) — also seen in diabetes. VDRL/RPR titre falls 4-fold (2 dilutions) within 6–12 months after adequate treatment — failure to fall suggests treatment failure, reinfection, or co-infection with HIV. Prozone phenomenon — false-negative VDRL in secondary syphilis due to very high antibody levels; if suspicion high, dilute serum 1:16 or 1:32 & retest. Penicillin is the only drug proven effective for syphilis in pregnancy & neurosyphilis — desensitise penicillin-allergic pregnant women. Always test for HIV in syphilis patients (co-infection common; HIV accelerates syphilis progression & may cause treatment failure). Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction — warn patient; self-limiting; antipyretics. Syphilis is resurging globally — especially in MSM, HIV-positive, and bisexual men; screen high-risk groups annually.

Introduction

Neurocysticercosis (NCC) — infection of the central nervous system by the larval stage of Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) — is the most common parasitic disease of the CNS worldwide and the leading cause of acquired epilepsy in adults in endemic regions (Latin America, India, sub-Saharan Africa, China, SE Asia).

Etiology

  • Taenia solium — pork tapeworm.
    • Definitive host — human (adult tapeworm in small intestine; taeniasis).
    • Intermediate host — pig (cysticercus cellulosae in muscle); humans (accidental — cysticercosis).
  • Humans develop NCC by ingesting T. solium eggs (faecal-oral route) — NOT by eating undercooked pork (that causes intestinal taeniasis).
  • Sources of eggs — food/water contaminated with human faeces from a tapeworm carrier; autoinfection (reverse peristalsis brings gravid proglottids/eggs from intestine to stomach; or faecal-oral self-infection).
  • Eggs hatch in stomach & upper small intestine → oncospheres (hexacanth embryos) penetrate intestinal wall → enter bloodstream → disseminate to brain, eye, muscle, subcutaneous tissue → develop into cysticerci (fluid-filled cysts with invaginated scolex).

Types of Cysts in Brain

  • Parenchymal — most common; cerebral cortex (especially near grey-white junction); single or multiple; size 5–20 mm.
  • Subarachnoid/intraventricular — basal cisterns; may cause hydrocephalus; racemose (grape-like, no scolex) form in basal cisterns.
  • Intraventricular — 4th ventricle most common; obstructive hydrocephalus; can be fatal.
  • Spinal cord — rare; subarachnoid or intramedullary.
  • Ocular — subretinal, vitreous; visual loss.
  • Stages of cyst evolution:
    1. Vesicular — viable cyst; clear fluid; viable scolex; minimal inflammation (immune evasion).
    2. Colloidal vesicular — degenerating cyst; turbid fluid; surrounding inflammation (oedema); clinical symptoms begin.
    3. Granular nodular — cyst retracts; oedema decreases; scolex calcifies.
    4. Calcified — dead cyst; calcified nodule; no oedema; may still cause seizures (focus of gliosis).

Clinical Manifestations

Depends on number, location, size, and stage of cysts; immune response of host.

1. Seizures — Most Common Presentation

  • Acute symptomatic seizures — when cyst degenerates (colloidal stage); inflammatory oedema irritates cortex → focal seizures with or without secondary generalisation; most common presentation (~70–80% of patients).
  • Late-onset seizures — after cyst calcifies; gliosis around calcified lesion acts as epileptic focus; may persist for years.
  • NCC is the most common cause of adult-onset partial epilepsy in endemic areas.

2. Headache

  • Due to raised intracranial pressure (multiple cysts, hydrocephalus, arachnoiditis) or cyst degeneration.
  • Migraine-like or tension-type; chronic.

3. Raised Intracranial Pressure

  • Multiple parenchymal cysts with oedema; intraventricular cyst with obstructive hydrocephalus; racemose cyst in basal cisterns causing communicating hydrocephalus.
  • Papilloedema, nausea, vomiting, altered sensorium; sixth nerve palsy (false localising sign).
  • Cysticercal encephalitis — diffuse brain oedema in patients with massive cyst load; life-threatening.

4. Meningitis

  • Chronic cysticercal arachnoiditis — chronic basal meningitis; lymphocytic pleocytosis in CSF; may mimic TB meningitis.
  • Cranial nerve palsies (especially II, III, VI, VII, VIII); communicating hydrocephalus.

5. Focal Neurological Deficits

  • Stroke — cysticercal vasculitis (inflammation of arteries in subarachnoid space); small vessel ischaemic stroke.
  • Cranial nerve palsy.
  • Spinal cord compression (rare).

6. Cognitive & Psychiatric

  • Dementia, behavioural changes (especially in chronic NCC with multiple calcifications).
  • Developmental delay in children.

7. Ocular Cysticercosis

  • Subretinal cyst — visual loss, retinal detachment.
  • Vitreous cyst — floaters, visual disturbance.
  • Conjunctival, extraocular muscle cyst — pain, diplopia.

8. Subcutaneous/Muscular Cysticercosis

  • Palpable subcutaneous nodules (rice-grain size); painless; may calcify (visible on X-ray as elliptical "cigar-shaped" calcifications in muscle).

Diagnosis

1. Neuroimaging — CT / MRI

  • CT findings:
    • Vesicular stage — cyst with scolex ("hole-with-dot" sign); CSF-density cyst in brain parenchyma; no oedema.
    • Colloidal stage — ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding oedema; scolex may be visible.
    • Granular stage — shrinking cyst; less oedema; nodular enhancement.
    • Calcified stage — small hyperdense calcified nodules (1–5 mm); no oedema; no enhancement.
    • Multiple cysts — "starry sky" appearance.
    • Hydrocephalus, basal arachnoiditis — in subarachnoid/intraventricular NCC.
  • MRI findings:
    • Better than CT for:
      • Intraventricular cysts (CSF flow void; may need CISS/FIESTA sequence).
      • Subarachnoid cysts (basal cisterns).
      • Spinal cysts.
      • Scolex ("hole-with-dot") — hyperintense on T1, hypointense on T2.
      • Oedema assessment.
    • Vesicular cyst — CSF signal on T1 & T2; scolex visible as eccentric nodule.
    • Colloidal cyst — T1 hyperintense (proteinaceous fluid); T2 hyperintense with surrounding oedema; ring enhancement post-gadolinium.
    • Calcified — hypointense on T2* (susceptibility sequence); may be missed on routine MRI — CT better for calcifications.

2. Immunological Tests

  • ELISA for anti-cysticercal antibodies — serum; sensitivity 65–85%; specificity 90% (lower in endemic areas due to background seroprevalence).
  • EITB (Enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot) — CDC-50 kd lentil lectin-agglutinated glycoprotein blot:
    • Gold standard serology; sensitivity 98% (multiple cysts), 60–70% (single cyst).
    • Specificity 100%.
    • Detects antibodies to 7 specific T. solium glycoproteins (50, 42–48, 39, 24, 21, 14, 13 kDa); positive if any one band present.
  • CSF ELISA / EITB — more sensitive than serum for subarachnoid/intraventricular NCC; CSF eosinophilia supportive.
  • Antigen detection — detects circulating cysticercal antigen (HP10 antigen); useful for viable cysts; monitors treatment response. Monoclonal antibody-based.

3. Stool Examination

  • Detect T. solium eggs or proglottids in stool — identifies tapeworm carrier (source of eggs); treat carrier to prevent autoinfection & spread.
  • Eggs — spherical, 30–40 µm, thick brown striated embryophore with hexacanth embryo (oncosphere) with 3 pairs of hooklets; indistinguishable from T. saginata eggs.
  • Proglottids — T. solium has 7–13 lateral uterine branches per side; T. saginata has 15–20.
  • Sensitive — perianal swab (NIH swab) or Scotch tape test.

4. Other Tests

  • CSF analysis — pleocytosis (lymphocytic/eosinophilic), raised protein, low glucose (in arachnoiditis); positive CSF EITB.
  • X-ray soft tissue (thigh, calf) — "cigar-shaped" or "rice-grain" calcifications in muscle (pathognomonic).
  • Biopsy of subcutaneous nodule — cysticercus cellulosae (cyst with invaginated scolex, hooklets).
  • Fundus examination — to exclude ocular cysticercosis (before starting antiparasitic treatment; ocular cysts can be worsened by albendazole → irreversible blindness).

5. Diagnostic Criteria — Del Brutto et al. (Revised 2017)

Absolute (1): cysticercal cyst on biopsy or imaging (scolex within cyst).

Neuroimaging (major): lesion with scolex; multilobulated cyst in basal cisterns; enhancing lesion; calcification(s).

Clinical (major): seizures; typical CT/MRI features.

Immunological (major): EITB positive.

Epidemiological (minor): household contact with T. solium; travel to endemic area.

Definitive diagnosis — 1 absolute OR 2 major + 1 minor + imaging.

Treatment

1. Antiparasitic Therapy

  • Albendazole 15 mg/kg/day (max 1200 mg/day) in 2 divided doses × 7–14 days — drug of choice; kills cysts by inhibiting microtubule polymerisation.
  • Praziquantel 50–100 mg/kg/day in 3 divided doses × 15 days — alternative.
  • Combination (albendazole + praziquantel) — more effective for multiple cysts.
  • Contraindicated: ocular cysticercosis (irreversible blindness from inflammation); spinal cord cyst (risk of oedema → paralysis) — surgical removal preferred.
  • Indications: viable cysts (vesicular & colloidal stages); multiple cysts; symptomatic subarachnoid cysts.
  • Not indicated for calcified cysts (dead cysts — no antiparasitic effect; just seizure management).

2. Corticosteroids

  • Dexamethasone or prednisolone — given before & during antiparasitic therapy to prevent inflammatory response to dying cysts (oedema → raised ICP → seizures, encephalitis).
  • Dexamethasone 8–12 mg/day starting 1–2 days before albendazole; continue for 4–7 days, then taper.
  • For cysticercal encephalitis — high-dose IV steroids; delay antiparasitic until oedema controlled.

3. Anticonvulsants

  • Levetiracetam, phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate — for seizure control.
  • Continue for 1–2 years after seizure-free; may be lifelong if calcified lesion remains epileptogenic.
  • Withdrawal of AED after calcification — controversial; recurrence risk ~40%.

4. Surgical / Interventional

  • VP shunt — for hydrocephalus (intraventricular cyst, basal arachnoiditis); may need revision (shunt malfunction from high CSF protein).
  • Neuroendoscopic removal — for intraventricular cysts; preferred over open surgery.
  • Resective surgery — for drug-resistant epilepsy with calcified epileptic focus.
  • Ocular cysticercosis — surgical removal (vitrectomy); no antiparasitic.
  • Spinal cyst — surgical decompression & removal.

5. Symptomatic & Supportive

  • Osmotic agents (mannitol) for raised ICP.
  • Analgesics for headache.
  • Treat tapeworm carrier (source) — niclosamide or praziquantel single dose.

Prevention

  • Proper sanitation & safe water.
  • Avoid eating undercooked pork (kills cysticerci).
  • Wash hands before eating; wash vegetables thoroughly.
  • Treat tapeworm carriers — screen household contacts of NCC patients.
  • Pig vaccination (TSOL18 vaccine) & deworming (oxfendazole) — control in endemic areas.
  • Meat inspection; proper cooking (≥60 °C internal temperature); freezing (-10 °C × 4 days) kills cysticerci.
  • Health education.

Clinical Pearl

NCC is the most common cause of adult-onset partial epilepsy in India — always suspect in any adult presenting with new-onset seizures, especially from an endemic area (UP, Bihar, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh). The "hole-with-dot" sign (cyst with eccentric scolex) on CT/MRI is pathognomonic. Always examine fundus before starting albendazole — ocular cysticercosis can be worsened by antiparasitic-induced inflammation → irreversible blindness; requires surgical removal. Always give corticosteroids (dexamethasone) before & during antiparasitic therapy — dying cysts release antigens causing intense inflammation → oedema, raised ICP, seizures, encephalitis. Calcified cysts do not require antiparasitic treatment — they are dead; treat seizures with anticonvulsants only. Intraventricular cysts require neuroendoscopic removal (not antiparasitic) — risk of sudden hydrocephalus & death if cyst obstructs foramen of Monro or 4th ventricle. CSF EITB is more sensitive than serum for subarachnoid/intraventricular NCC. Always check stool of patient & household contacts for T. solium eggs — the tapeworm carrier is the source of eggs; treating the carrier prevents further transmission & autoinfection. Pig vaccination & deworming in endemic areas is the most effective public health intervention — India's National Taeniasis/Cysticercosis Control Programme is being piloted in high-burden districts.
