Introduction

Rabies — a fatal acute viral encephalomyelitis caused by Lyssavirus (family Rhabdoviridae) — is transmitted through saliva of rabid animals (dogs in 99% of human cases; also cats, monkeys, bats, foxes, jackals, mongooses, cows). Once symptoms appear, rabies is virtually 100% fatal. Therefore, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) immediately after exposure is the only way to prevent death. India accounts for ~36% of global rabies deaths (~20,000 annually).

Categories of Exposure (WHO)

Category Type of exposure Recommended PEP
ITouching, feeding animal; licks on intact skinNone — wash with soap & water; no vaccine
IINibbling uncovered skin; minor scratches without bleedingWound care + vaccine (no RIG)
IIISingle/multiple bites/scratches that break skin; contamination of mucous membrane with saliva; licks on broken skin; exposure to bats; head/neck bitesWound care + RIG + vaccine

Steps in PEP

Step 1 — Immediate Wound Care (most important & often neglected)

  1. Wash wound immediately & thoroughly with soap & running water for at least 15 minutes — mechanical removal of virus.
  2. Then wash with povidone-iodine or 70% alcohol — virucidal action.
  3. Do NOT suture the wound — if unavoidable, delay suturing; infiltrate wound with RIG first.
  4. Do NOT apply irritants — chillies, oil, turmeric, lime (traditional remedies; harmful; increase viral spread).
  5. Apply sterile dressing.
  6. Tetanus prophylaxis — tetanus toxoid + TIG if indicated.
  7. Antibiotics — broad-spectrum (amoxicillin-clavulanate; or doxycycline + metronidazole) if wound infected or deep puncture; cover Pasteurella, anaerobes, S. aureus, Capnocytophaga.

Step 2 — Rabies Immunoglobulin (RIG) — for Category III exposure

  • Equine Rabies Immunoglobulin (ERIG) — 40 IU/kg body weight; cheaper; risk of serum sickness & anaphylaxis (skin test required previously; WHO now says no skin test needed if properly purified).
  • Human Rabies Immunoglobulin (HRIG) — 20 IU/kg body weight; safer; more expensive; no skin test required.
  • Administration:
    • Infiltrate as much as possible into & around the wound — neutralises virus at site of inoculation.
    • Remaining dose — IM at distant site (deltoid or anterolateral thigh; NOT gluteal — fat reduces absorption).
    • If multiple wounds — dilute RIG with sterile normal saline to infiltrate all wounds.
    • If wound is on a digit — infiltrate carefully (avoid compartment syndrome); use a 25-gauge needle.
    • Must be given within 7 days of first vaccine dose — after that, antibody from vaccine is forming; RIG not needed.
  • Contraindication — RIG is given once in lifetime; never repeat (immune complex disease).

Step 3 — Rabies Vaccine — Active Immunisation

Types of Vaccine
  • Modern cell-culture vaccines (CCV):
    • HDCV (Human Diploid Cell Vaccine) — Mérieux; gold standard; expensive.
    • PCECV (Purified Chick Embryo Cell Vaccine) — Rabipur; widely used.
    • PDEV (Purified Duck Embryo Vaccine) — Vaxirab.
    • Vero cell vaccine — Abhayrab, Indirab; cost-effective; widely used in India.
    • Recombinant vaccine — experimental.
  • Nerve tissue vaccine (NTV) — Semple vaccine (sheep brain — BPL-inactivated); obsolete & not recommended by WHO; still used in some Indian government centres due to cost; high risk of neuroparalytic complications (1 in 200–2000).
Dose & Route
  • Single dose — 1 vial (1.0 mL) regardless of age or weight (intramuscular) OR 0.1 mL (intradermal).
  • Reconstitute immediately before use; discard if not used within 6 hours.
Routes of Administration
  • Intramuscular (IM):
    • Adult & child >2 years — deltoid muscle (arm).
    • Child <2 years — anterolateral thigh.
    • NEVER gluteal — fat reduces absorption; lower immunogenicity.
  • Intradermal (ID):
    • 0.1 mL at one site (raises a visible & palpable bleb).
    • WHO pre-qualifies ID route — cost-saving (60–80% less vaccine); immunogenic equivalent to IM.
    • Used in India, Thailand, Sri Lanka, Philippines.
    • Site — deltoid (adults); anterolateral thigh (children <2 years).
    • Contraindicated — chloroquine therapy (reduces ID response; use IM), immunosuppression.
Schedules
Schedule Route Days Indication
Essen (5-dose IM)IM, deltoidDays 0, 3, 7, 14, 28 (5 doses)Standard PEP — previously unvaccinated
Essen (4-dose IM)IM, deltoidDays 0 (2 sites), 7, 21Alternative
Updated Thai Red Cross (2-2-2-0-2 ID)ID, 2 sitesDays 0, 3, 7, 28 (2 injections per visit at 2 different sites) — total 8 injectionsStandard ID PEP — WHO recommended
IPC (1-week ID)ID, 2 sitesDays 0, 3, 7 — 2 injections per visitShorter schedule; WHO approved 2018
4-site IDID, 4 sites on day 0 + 1 site days 7 & 28Day 0 (4 sites), Day 7 (1 site), Day 28 (1 site)Alternative
Previously vaccinated (any PEP schedule)IM (1 dose) or ID (2 sites)Days 0 & 3 — 2 doses onlyFor re-exposure — no RIG needed

Step 4 — Observe the Animal

  • If dog/cat available for observation — confine & observe for 10 days.
    • If animal remains healthy for 10 days — rabies ruled out; can discontinue vaccination after day 3 (no need for full course).
    • If animal dies or shows rabies signs — continue full course + RIG.
  • For other animals (wild, stray, livestock) — assume rabid; give full PEP.
  • If animal escapes — assume rabid; full PEP.
  • Laboratory confirmation of animal — fluorescent antibody test (FAT) on brain tissue (hippocampus, cerebellum, brainstem); mouse inoculation test (historical); PCR (research).

Step 5 — Special Situations

  • Previously vaccinated patients — 2 doses on days 0 & 3 (IM or ID); NO RIG.
  • Immunocompromised patients — full course + RIG (Category II & III); check seroconversion (neutralising antibody titre ≥0.5 IU/mL) 2–4 weeks after last dose; if inadequate, repeat dose.
  • Pregnancy — not a contraindication; rabies vaccine & RIG are safe.
  • Infants & children — same dose as adults (ID 0.1 mL; IM 1.0 mL); site varies.
  • HIV-positive — full course; check seroconversion; consider extra dose if CD4 <200.
  • Chloroquine therapy — avoid ID route; use IM.
  • Delayed presentation — even months/years after exposure, start PEP (incubation may be prolonged).

Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) — for High-Risk Individuals

  • Veterinarians, animal handlers, laboratory staff, travellers to endemic areas, children in endemic areas.
  • Schedule — days 0, 7, 21 (or 0, 7, 28); IM (1 mL) or ID (0.1 mL).
  • Booster — every 2–5 years; or check antibody titre (<0.5 IU/mL → booster).
  • If exposed later — only 2 doses on days 0 & 3 (no RIG needed).

Failure of PEP — Causes

  • Delay in initiating treatment.
  • Incomplete/inadequate wound care.
  • Failure to give RIG (Category III).
  • Incorrect RIG administration (not infiltrated into wound).
  • Incorrect vaccine schedule or route (gluteal injection).
  • Immunosuppression (HIV, steroids, malignancy).
  • Use of chloroquine with ID route.
  • Use of NT vaccine (Semple).
  • Severe facial/neck wounds (short incubation; virus reaches CNS before antibody).

Prevention

  • Vaccinate dogs — mass dog vaccination (>70% coverage) interrupts transmission; most effective public health intervention.
  • Stray dog control — animal birth control (ABC) programme.
  • Public education — wash wounds immediately; seek medical care; avoid traditional remedies; vaccinate pets.
  • PrEP for high-risk groups.
  • Surveillance — report animal bites; track rabies cases.

Clinical Pearl

Rabies is 100% fatal once symptoms appear — PEP must be started immediately after exposure. The single most important intervention is thorough wound washing with soap & water for 15 minutes — mechanical removal of virus reduces infection risk by up to 90%, yet is often neglected. For Category III exposure (bite breaking skin, mucosal contamination, head/neck, bat exposure) — give BOTH RIG and vaccine. RIG provides passive immunity (neutralising antibody at wound site) during the 7–10 days before vaccine-induced antibody appears. Infiltrate RIG into & around the wound — if dose insufficient for all wounds, dilute with saline; if wound on digit, use 25-gauge needle to avoid compartment syndrome. Never inject RIG & vaccine at the same site — RIG will neutralise vaccine. Never give RIG after day 7 of vaccination — antibody already forming; RIG can cause immune complex disease. Never inject vaccine in the gluteal region — fat reduces absorption; use deltoid (adults & children ≥2 yr) or anterolateral thigh (infants). Intradermal route saves 60–80% of vaccine cost — India's National Rabies Control Programme uses ID route widely. Observe dog for 10 days — if healthy, discontinue vaccination after day 3. The Milwaukee Protocol (induced coma + antiviral cocktails) has saved ~5 patients worldwide with clinical rabies — experimental, not standard; PEP remains the only reliable prevention. India's National Action Plan for Dog Mediated Rabies Elimination (NAPRE) by 2030 aims to eliminate rabies through mass dog vaccination & PEP access.

Introduction

Tetanus is an acute fatal disease caused by Clostridium tetani — a Gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-forming, drumstick-shaped bacillus — through its exotoxin tetanospasmin (a neurotoxin that blocks inhibitory neurotransmitter release at spinal synapses, causing severe muscle spasms). Diagnosis is clinical; lab tests are supportive.

Laboratory Diagnosis

1. Specimen

  • Wound swab/pus from entry wound (umbilical stump in neonatal tetanus, post-natal septic abortion, surgical wound, chronic ulcer, injection site).
  • Tissue biopsy from wound edge.
  • CSF — usually normal (helps exclude other causes of meningismus); no organisms.

2. Direct Microscopy

  • Gram stain — Gram-positive bacilli with terminal drumstick-shaped spores (round terminal spore gives characteristic drumstick appearance); may be Gram-variable in old cultures.
  • Spores are heat-resistant (boil 100 °C × 1 h survives); survive in soil for years.
  • Limit — microscopy alone is non-diagnostic (C. tetani may be present in normal flora; morphology alone cannot confirm toxin production).

3. Culture

  • Robertson's cooked meat (RCM) broth — anaerobic; C. tetani grows with gas, digests meat slowly; produces "drumstick" bacilli.
  • Blood agar — anaerobic incubation; swarming growth (translucent film) due to motility; important to identify.
  • Nitrate-mannitol agar — selective.
  • Trypticase sulfite neomycin agar.
  • Incubation — 37 °C, 24–48 h, anaerobic (GasPak jar, anaerobic chamber).

4. Identification

  • Gram stain — terminal drumstick spores; Gram-positive bacilli.
  • Motility — motile (swarming on blood agar).
  • Biochemical tests — indole positive, nitrate negative, gelatin liquefaction positive, no sugar fermentation.
  • Toxigenicity testing — most important.
    • Animal inoculation (mouse bioassay) — gold standard; inject culture filtrate into mice: one group unprotected, one protected with tetanus antitoxin. Unprotected mice develop tetanic spasms & die; protected mice survive.
    • PCR — detects tetX gene (toxin gene); faster but not widely available.
    • ELISA — detects toxin in culture filtrate.

5. Serology

  • Anti-tetanus antibody titre — to assess immune status; ≥0.1 IU/mL is protective.
  • Useful for diagnosing inadequate immunity in patients with tetanus (most have <0.01 IU/mL).
  • Not diagnostic of acute disease — tetanus toxin is so potent that disease can occur without measurable antibody response.

6. Other Tests

  • Clinical diagnosis — based on trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus, opisthotonus, muscle spasms, intact sensorium, normal CSF.
  • CBC — leucocytosis.
  • Electromyography (EMG) — continuous motor unit discharges; loss of silent period after masseter reflex.
  • Wound culture — supports diagnosis but not necessary if clinical signs present.

1. Active Immunisation — Tetanus Toxoid (TT)

  • Toxoid — formaldehyde-treated tetanospasmin; loses toxicity but retains antigenicity; adsorbed on aluminium hydroxide adjuvant.
  • Types
    • DTP — diphtheria + tetanus + whole-cell pertussis.
    • DTaP — diphtheria + tetanus + acellular pertussis.
    • Td / Tdap — reduced-dose diphtheria + tetanus ± acellular pertussis (booster for adolescents/adults).
    • TT (tetanus toxoid alone) — for adults.
    • Pentavalent vaccine — DTP + Hepatitis B + Hib (used in India's UIP).
  • Schedule (India — NIS):
    • Primary — 3 doses at 6, 10, 14 weeks.
    • Boosters — at 16–18 months & 5 years.
    • Then Td at 10 & 16 years.
    • Adults — booster every 10 years (Td).
  • Efficacy — >95% after complete primary series; wanes over 10 years.
  • Pregnancy — Td given during each pregnancy (2 doses in 1st pregnancy; 1 dose in subsequent); protects neonate via transplacental antibody.

  • Equine tetanus antitoxin (ATS) — 1500 IU SC/IM after skin test (cheaper; risk of serum sickness; mostly replaced by HTIG in modern practice).

  • Neutralise unbound toxin — HTIG 3000–6000 IU IM (or IV preparation) — neutralises circulating toxin only (does NOT reverse bound toxin); give ASAP.
  • Eliminate organism — IV Metronidazole 500 mg QID × 7–10 days (drug of choice); Penicillin G (alternative; theoretical concern — GABA antagonist may worsen spasms); debride wound.

  • Autonomic dysfunction — labetalol, morphine, clonidine for sympathetic overactivity; atropine for bradycardia.

  • Proper wound care — clean with soap & water; debride necrotic tissue; remove foreign bodies.
  • Sterile technique in surgery & deliveries.
  • Safe abortion & clean cord care in newborns.
  • Health education.

Tetanus is a clinical diagnosis — do NOT wait for lab confirmation. The classic tetrad is trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus (sardonic smile), opisthotonus, and intact sensorium. The incubation period inversely correlates with severity — <7 days portends severe disease & poor prognosis. Neonatal tetanus — from cutting umbilical cord with unsterile instrument or applying cow dung/ash — remains a leading cause of neonatal mortality in unimmunised populations; preventable by maternal TT immunisation & clean delivery practices. Cephalic tetanus — cranial nerve palsies (especially VII) after head/face wound or otitis media; may progress to generalised tetanus. Always immunise recovered tetanus patients — the disease does not confer immunity (toxin dose too small); full primary TT series is mandatory. Magnesium sulphate infusion is now standard adjunct for severe tetanus — controls spasms & autonomic dysfunction; reduces need for mechanical ventilation. Metronidazole is preferred over penicillin — penicillin is a GABA antagonist that may worsen spasms. India's Maternal & Neonatal Tetanus Elimination (MNTE) — achieved WHO elimination status in 2015 (<1 case per 1000 live births in every district) through universal TT immunisation of pregnant women & clean delivery practices.

Introduction

Vaginal candidiasis (vulvovaginal candidiasis — VVC) is a fungal infection of the vulva & vagina caused by Candida species — most commonly Candida albicans (~85–90%). Affects ~75% of women at least once in lifetime; 5–8% develop recurrent VVC (≥4 episodes/year).

Etiology

  • Candida albicans — most common (~85–90%); forms germ tubes & chlamydospores.
  • Non-albicans Candida — C. glabrata (5–10%; increasingly resistant to azoles), C. tropicalis, C. parapsilosis, C. krusei (intrinsic fluconazole resistance), C. lusitaniae (amphotericin B resistance).
  • Candida — dimorphic fungus; yeast form in vagina; forms pseudohyphae & true hyphae in tissue; budding yeast (blastoconidia) 3–6 µm.
  • Normal commensal of vagina in ~20% of women; overgrowth causes infection.

Risk Factors

  • Antibiotic use — destroys normal vaginal lactobacilli → loss of acidic pH → Candida overgrowth (most common risk factor).
  • Pregnancy — high oestrogen → increased glycogen in vaginal epithelium → Candida growth; 2–10× more common.
  • Diabetes mellitus — uncontrolled; high vaginal glucose.
  • Immunosuppression — HIV/AIDS, steroids, chemotherapy, malignancy.
  • Oestrogen-containing oral contraceptives or hormone replacement therapy.
  • Intrauterine device (IUD).
  • Poor hygiene, tight synthetic underwear (warm, moist environment).
  • Douching — disrupts normal flora.
  • Iron deficiency anaemia, hypothyroidism, Cushing's syndrome.

Clinical Features

  • Pruritus vulvae — intense itching; most prominent symptom.
  • Vaginal discharge — thick, white, curdy ("cottage cheese"-like), odourless; adherent to vaginal walls.
  • Burning — vulva, especially on urination (dysuria) or intercourse (dyspareunia).
  • Erythema & oedema of vulva & vagina; fissures, excoriations from scratching.
  • Satellite lesions — pustules surrounding erythematous area on vulva/perineum.
  • Vaginal pH — normal (4.0–4.5); distinguishes from bacterial vaginosis (pH >4.5) and trichomoniasis (pH >5.0).
  • Whiff test (KOH) — negative (distinguishes from BV — positive "fishy" odour).

Laboratory Diagnosis

1. Clinical Specimen

  • Vaginal discharge — collected with speculum using sterile swab; from posterior fornix & lateral vaginal wall.

2. Direct Microscopy

  • Wet mount (saline) — budding yeast cells (3–6 µm), pseudohyphae; few WBCs.
  • 10% KOH mount — dissolves epithelial cells & debris; easier to see yeast & pseudohyphae (sensitivity 50–70%).
  • Gram stain — Gram-positive budding yeast cells & pseudohyphae; sensitivity higher than wet mount (~80%).

3. Culture

  • Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) — creamy white pasty colonies in 24–48 h at 37 °C.
  • Chromogenic Candida agar (CHROMagar) — differentiates species by colony colour:
    • C. albicans — green.
    • C. tropicalis — blue/purple.
    • C. krusei — pink, fuzzy.
    • C. glabrata — pink/white.
    • C. parapsilosis — cream/pink.
  • Culture is more sensitive than microscopy — detects low-grade infection; but positive culture alone does not prove infection (20% colonisation); must correlate with symptoms.

4. Identification

  • Germ tube test — subculture in human/animal serum at 37 °C × 2–3 h; C. albicans forms germ tubes (short hyphal projections); >95% specific.
  • Chlamydospore formation — on corn meal agar; C. albicans forms chlamydospores at tips of pseudohyphae.
  • Sugar fermentation & assimilation tests — identify species.
  • API 20C AUX — commercial identification system.
  • MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry — rapid identification.
  • PCR — species identification; PNA FISH.

5. Other Tests

  • Vaginal pH measurement — normal (4.0–4.5) in candidiasis; elevated in BV & trichomoniasis.
  • Whiff (amine) test — KOH added to discharge; negative in candidiasis (positive "fishy" in BV).
  • STD screen — for recurrent or atypical cases; rule out co-infections (HIV, diabetes check).
  • Blood glucose — if recurrent; rule out diabetes.
  • HIV test — if recurrent, severe, or non-albicans species.

Bacterial vaginosisThin, grey, homogenous, "fishy" odour>4.5Positive (fishy)Clue cells
TrichomoniasisYellow-green, frothy, malodorous>5.0VariableMotile trichomonads, many WBCs

Uncomplicated VVC (immunocompetent, mild-moderate, <4 episodes/year, C. albicans)

  • Topical azoles (intravaginal) — clotrimazole 1% cream 5 g PV × 7–14 days; miconazole 2% cream 5 g PV × 7 days; tioconazole 6.5% ointment PV single dose; terconazole 0.4% cream × 7 days or 0.8% × 3 days; butoconazole 2% sustained release × 1 dose.
  • Oral — fluconazole 150 mg single oral dose — preferred for convenience; alternative itraconazole 200 mg BD × 1 day.
  • Cure rate 80–95%.

Complicated VVC (severe, recurrent, pregnancy, diabetes, non-albicans)

  • Severe (extensive erythema, oedema, fissures) — fluconazole 150 mg PO × 2 doses (72 h apart); or topical azole × 7–14 days.
  • Recurrent VVC (≥4 episodes/year) — induction with fluconazole 150 mg every 3 days × 3 doses; then maintenance fluconazole 150 mg weekly × 6 months.
  • Pregnancy — topical azoles only (7-day course preferred); fluconazole contraindicated in 1st trimester (teratogenic).
  • Non-albicans Candida — often azole-resistant; treat with terconazole or boric acid 600 mg PV capsule daily × 14 days (effective against C. glabrata); amphotericin B suppository rare.
  • HIV — same regimen; recurrent disease common; suppressive fluconazole weekly.

Prevention

  • Avoid unnecessary antibiotics.
  • Wear loose cotton underwear; avoid tight synthetic clothing.
  • Avoid douching; maintain natural flora.
  • Control diabetes; check blood glucose.
  • Avoid prolonged wet swimsuits; dry genital area thoroughly.
  • Probiotics (Lactobacillus) — controversial; may help prevent recurrent VVC.
  • Treat sexual partner only if symptomatic (balanitis).

Clinical Pearl

The single most useful bedside diagnostic test is the 10% KOH mount — dissolves epithelial cells, allowing clear visualisation of budding yeast & pseudohyphae. Vaginal pH is the key differentiator — normal (4.0–4.5) in candidiasis; elevated (>4.5) in bacterial vaginosis & trichomoniasis. Fluconazole 150 mg single oral dose is the standard first-line for uncomplicated VVC — convenient, effective, well-tolerated; 80–95% cure rate. Recurrent VVC (≥4 episodes/year) — check HIV, diabetes, thyroid; consider maintenance fluconazole weekly × 6 months. Non-albicans Candida (especially C. glabrata & C. krusei) are often fluconazole-resistant — use boric acid vaginal capsules (600 mg PV daily × 14 days) or terconazole. Pregnancy — topical azoles only (7-day course); avoid oral fluconazole (teratogenic in 1st trimester — case-control studies show increased risk of miscarriage & congenital anomalies). Always exclude diabetes in recurrent VVC — uncontrolled diabetes is the most common underlying cause; control blood glucose to prevent recurrences. Asymptomatic Candida colonisation does not require treatment — 20% of women have Candida in vagina without symptoms; treat only symptomatic cases.

Clinical Identification

The 28-year-old woman with high-grade fever, vomiting, flank pain, and likely urinary symptoms (dysuria, frequency, urgency) — consistent with acute pyelonephritis (upper urinary tract infection). If lower urinary symptoms alone — acute cystitis. Women are at higher risk due to short urethra & proximity to anus.

Definition

Urinary tract infection (UTI) is an infection of any part of the urinary tract — bladder (cystitis), urethra (urethritis), prostate (prostatitis), kidneys (pyelonephritis). Most common bacterial infection in women; ~50% of women experience UTI in their lifetime.

Classification

  • By site — lower (cystitis, urethritis); upper (pyelonephritis).
  • By complexity — uncomplicated (healthy non-pregnant adult woman); complicated (pregnancy, male, child, catheter, urinary abnormality, diabetes, immunosuppression, recent instrumentation, recurrent, severe).
  • By acquisition — community-acquired; catheter-associated (CAUTI).

Organism Frequency Comment
E. coli75–85%Most common; uropathogenic strains with P fimbriae (pyelonephritis), K1 capsule, haemolysin, siderophores
Klebsiella pneumoniae5–10%Diabetics, catheterised
Proteus mirabilis5%Urease producer → struvite stones; alkaline urine
Enterococcus faecalis3–5%Catheter, instrumentation
Staphylococcus saprophyticus5–10% (young women)Sexually active young women; coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant
Pseudomonas aeruginosa2–3%Catheterised, instrumentation, complicated
Enterobacter, Citrobacter, Serratia, Acinetobacter<5%Hospital-acquired, MDR

  1. Route — ascending (most common; periurethral flora → urethra → bladder → kidneys); haematogenous (S. aureus, TB); lymphatic (rare).
  2. Adherence — uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) with type 1 fimbriae (binds uroplakin on bladder epithelium — cystitis) & P fimbriae (binds globoside on renal epithelium — pyelonephritis).
  3. Host defences — urinary flow (flushing); acidic pH; osmolality; Tamm-Horsfall protein (uromodulin); secretory IgA; bladder mucopolysaccharide; neutrophils.
  4. Risk factors:
    • Female sex (short urethra, proximity to anus).
    • Sexual activity ("honeymoon cystitis"); diaphragm + spermicide use.
    • Pregnancy (progesterone → ureteral dilatation & reflux; mechanical obstruction).
    • Postmenopause (loss of oestrogen → loss of lactobacilli → vaginal pH rises).
    • Urinary obstruction — stones, BPH, strictures, tumours, reflux (VUR).
    • Catheterisation (most common hospital risk).
    • Diabetes (immunocompromise, glycosuria, neurogenic bladder).
    • Immunosuppression.
    • Instrumentation.

Lower UTI (Cystitis)

  • Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, haematuria.
  • Low-grade fever; no flank pain.

Upper UTI (Pyelonephritis)

  • High fever with chills & rigors.
  • Flank pain & costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness.
  • Nausea, vomiting.
  • Symptoms of cystitis may or may not be present.
  • Severe — sepsis, septic shock, ARDS.

1. Urine Specimen Collection

  • Clean-catch midstream urine (MSU) — most common; clean perineum; spread labia; discard first portion; collect midstream in sterile container.
  • Catheter specimen — from port (not from bag); preferred if catheterised.
  • Suprapubic aspiration — neonates & infants; sterile bladder puncture.
  • In-out catheterisation — if MSU not possible.
  • Transport — within 2 h; refrigerate (4 °C) if delayed; boric acid preservative.

2. Urinalysis (Dipstick)

  • Leukocyte esterase — detects pus cells (WBC esterase); sensitivity 75–95%; specificity 85–95%.
  • Nitrite — bacterial reduction of nitrate to nitrite (by Enterobacterales — E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterobacter); sensitivity 35–85%; specificity 95%; not produced by S. saprophyticus, Enterococcus, Pseudomonas.
  • Blood — haematuria (cystitis, stones, malignancy).
  • Protein — mild in UTI; nephrotic if heavy.
  • pH & specific gravity.

3. Urine Microscopy

  • Pyuria — >5–10 WBCs/HPF; indicates infection.
  • Bacteriuria — bacteria seen on Gram stain of uncentrifuged urine (≥1 organism/OIF correlates with ≥10⁵ CFU/mL).
  • Hematuria — RBCs.
  • Cast — WBC cast (pyelonephritis — distinguishes from cystitis).
  • Crystals — struvite (infection stones); calcium oxalate.

4. Urine Culture — Gold Standard

  • Semiquantitative culture — calibrated loop (0.001 mL or 0.01 mL) streaked on blood agar & MacConkey agar; incubated 37 °C × 24–48 h.
  • Significant bacteriuria:
    • ≥10⁵ CFU/mL — symptomatic women, asymptomatic (2 specimens), men.
    • ≥10⁴ CFU/mL — symptomatic women, catheterised.
    • ≥10² CFU/mL — symptomatic young women (acute cystitis); suprapubic aspirate (any number).
  • Identification — biochemical tests, MALDI-TOF, automated (Vitek 2).
  • Antibiotic susceptibility — disk diffusion or MIC; guide therapy.
  • Sterile pyuria — pyuria with negative culture — TB, Chlamydia, Ureaplasma, fungal, fastidious organisms, stones, tumour, NSAIDs.

  • Blood culture — in pyelonephritis, sepsis (positive in 10–20%).
  • CBG — leucocytosis.
  • Renal function — urea, creatinine (baseline; AKI in severe).
  • Blood glucose — rule out diabetes.
  • Imaging:
    • Ultrasound — for recurrent UTI, pyelonephritis, obstruction, stones, renal abscess.
    • CT abdomen — for complications (emphysematous pyelonephritis — diabetics; abscess; stones; obstruction).
    • MCUG (micturating cystourethrogram) — for children with recurrent UTI (VUR).

Uncomplicated Cystitis (Female)

  • Nitrofurantoin 100 mg BD × 5 days (first-line; safe in pregnancy).
  • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole) 960 mg BD × 3 days (first-line if local E. coli resistance <20%; avoid in pregnancy 1st trimester).
  • Fosfomycin 3 g single dose.
  • Pivmecillinam 400 mg BD × 3–7 days.
  • Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) — reserve; resistance rising.

Pyelonephritis (Mild — Outpatient)

  • Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD × 7 days OR levofloxacin 750 mg OD × 5 days.
  • Co-trimoxazole 960 mg BD × 14 days (if susceptible).
  • Cefixime 400 mg OD × 7 days (alternative).

Pyelonephritis (Severe — Hospitalised)

  • IV Ceftriaxone 1–2 g OD.
  • IV Ciprofloxacin 400 mg BD.
  • IV Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g 6-hourly (if MDR suspected).
  • IV Amoxicillin-clavulanate.
  • IV Carbapenem (meropenem) — if ESBL/CRE suspected.
  • Switch to oral when afebrile 24–48 h & clinically stable; total course 7–14 days.

Special Situations

  • Pregnancy — nitrofurantoin (avoid term — haemolysis in G6PD), cephalosporins (cephalexin); avoid fluoroquinolones, co-trimoxazole (1st & 3rd trimester), tetracyclines.
  • CAUTI — remove/change catheter; treat with antibiotics targeting Enterococcus, Pseudomonas, MDR organisms.
  • Recurrent UTI — investigate (postmenopausal, diabetes, stones); consider prophylactic nitrofurantoin or co-trimoxazole (low dose, post-coital or daily); vaginal oestrogen in postmenopause.
  • Catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria — do NOT treat (except pregnancy, urological procedure, neutropenia); antibiotic stewardship.

Prevention

  • Hydration — 2–3 L/day; frequent urination.
  • Post-coital voiding — flushes bacteria.
  • Wipe front to back.
  • Avoid spermicide/diaphragm in recurrent UTI.
  • Cranberry products (proanthocyanidins prevent E. coli adherence) — modest benefit.
  • Vaginal oestrogen (postmenopausal).
  • Probiotics (Lactobacillus).
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis — for recurrent UTI.
  • Vaccine (Uro-Vaxom — E. coli extract; Stirbaum; ExPEC4V conjugate in trials).
  • Catheter care — aseptic insertion, closed drainage, minimal dwell.

The single most important diagnostic test for UTI is urine culture with susceptibility testing — guides therapy, especially with rising antibiotic resistance. Significant bacteriuria is ≥10⁵ CFU/mL in asymptomatic women (2 specimens), ≥10⁴ CFU/mL in symptomatic women/catheterised, ≥10² CFU/mL in acute cystitis in young women. Sterile pyuria (pyuria + negative routine culture) — always consider M. tuberculosis (3 early morning urines for AFB), Chlamydia trachomatis, Ureaplasma, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, fungi, fastidious organisms; also non-infectious (NSAIDs, stones, tumour, interstitial nephritis).   • Klebsiella, other Gram-negative bacilli.

  • Neisseria meningitidis — adolescents; epidemics in sub-Saharan Africa meningitis belt.
  • Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) — where vaccine not used.
Children 5–18 yr & young adults
  • N. meningitidis — most common; dormitory, military, Hajj outbreaks.
  • S. pneumoniae.
Adults 18–50 yr
  • S. pneumoniae — most common.
  • N. meningitidis.
Adults >50 yr; alcoholics; immunocompromised
  • S. pneumoniae.
  • Listeria monocytogenes — increasing; cell-mediated immunity defect.
  • Gram-negative bacilli (including Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter in neurosurgery/post-trauma).
Post-neurosurgery; CSF shunt; head trauma
  • Coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS — S. epidermidis).
  • S. aureus.
  • Gram-negative bacilli (Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter).
  • Propionibacterium acnes (shunt).

  • Sickle cell disease, asplenia, complement deficiency (C5–C9) — N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae.
  • HIV, immunosuppression — Listeria, S. pneumoniae, Cryptococcus (fungal).
  • CSF leak (otorrhoea, rhinorrhoea) — S. pneumoniae.
  • Pneumococcal pneumonia, endocarditis.
  • Pregnancy — Listeria.
  • Alcoholism — S. pneumoniae, Listeria.

Clinical Features

  • Classic triad — fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status (present in >95% of cases when at least 2 of 3 present).
  • Headache — severe, generalized; photophobia.
  • Nausea, vomiting.
  • Altered sensorium — confusion, lethargy, seizures, coma.
  • Signs of meningeal irritation — neck stiffness, Kernig's sign (inability to extend knee when hip flexed at 90°), Brudzinski's sign (neck flexion → hip/knee flexion).
  • Petechial/purpuric rash — N. meningitidis (meningococcaemia); Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (adrenal haemorrhage, DIC, shock).
  • Focal neurological deficit — cranial nerve palsy, hemiparesis.

Lumbar Puncture
  • Site — L3–L4 or L4–L5 intervertebral space.
  • Contraindications:
    • Raised ICP with focal signs or papilloedema — risk of herniation; do CT head first.
    • Coagulopathy (INR >1.4; platelets <50,000).
    • Overlying skin infection.
    • Haemodynamically unstable.
  • Collect 3 tubes (1–2 mL each):
    • Tube 1 — cell count & differential.
    • Tube 2 — glucose & protein.
    • Tube 3 — Gram stain, culture, antigen tests, molecular.

  • Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) — protects against 13 serotypes; given in India's UIP.
  • Meningococcal vaccine:
    • Quadrivalent conjugate (A, C, Y, W135) — Menactra, Menveo; for Hajj pilgrims, military, asplenia, complement deficiency.
    • Men B vaccine (Bexsero, Trumenba) — for serogroup B.
  • BCG — protects against TB meningitis.

Clinical Pearl

Acute bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency — empiric antibiotics must be given within 1 hour of presentation; do NOT wait for LP or imaging if unstable or LP delayed. The classic triad of fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status is present in >95% (if at least 2 of 3). Give dexamethasone before or with first antibiotic dose — reduces hearing loss & neurological sequelae in S. pneumoniae meningitis (especially in high-income settings; less clear benefit in low-income). Repeat LP at 48–72 h if no clinical improvement (persistent fever, worsening mental status) — assess response; consider complications (subdural empyema, ventriculitis, abscess).

Introduction

Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS) is a constellation of birth defects caused by transplacental transmission of Rubella virus (family Togaviridae, genus Rubivirus) from a mother who acquires primary rubella infection during pregnancy. The classic Gregg triad (1941) — cataract, cardiac defects, deafness — defines the syndrome.

Etiology & Pathogenesis

  • Virus — Rubella virus (RNA, Togaviridae); humans only reservoir; transmitted by droplets & transplacentally.
  • Maternal infection — primary rubella during pregnancy (most damaging in 1st trimester).
  • Transplacental transmission — virus crosses placenta → infects fetus → causes:
    1. Cell division inhibition — slows fetal cell mitosis → growth retardation, organ hypoplasia.
    2. Chromosomal damage — breaks, apoptosis.
    3. Vasculitis — vascular injury in developing organs → stenosis, atresia, hypoplasia.
    4. Chronic persistent infection — virus remains in fetal tissues for months–years after birth; sheds in urine, saliva, CSF for up to 1–2 years.

Risk by Gestational Age

Gestational age at infection Risk of CRS Severity
1st 4 weeks90%Most severe; multiple defects; spontaneous abortion
5–8 weeks50–80%Severe; multiple defects
9–12 weeks25–35%Single defect (often deafness)
13–16 weeks10–20%Usually deafness only
17–20 weeks5–10%Rare; mild
>20 weeks<1%Rare; normal outcome

Clinical Features

1. Classic Triad (Gregg Triad)

  1. Sensorineural deafness
    • Most common manifestation (~60–75% of CRS).
    • May be unilateral or bilateral; progressive.
    • Cochlear damage (organ of Corti).
  2. Ocular abnormalities
    • Cataract — bilateral or unilateral; nuclear; "pearl-like".
    • Congenital glaucoma — cloudy cornea, buphthalmos.
    • Pigmentary retinopathy — "salt-and-pepper" appearance; most common ocular finding.
    • Microphthalmia, strabismus.
  3. Congenital heart disease
    • Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) — most common cardiac defect.
    • Pulmonary artery stenosis.
    • Ventricular septal defect (VSD); tetralogy of Fallot.

2. Other Features

  • Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) — small for gestational age.
  • Thrombocytopenic purpura — "blueberry muffin baby" (extramedullary haematopoiesis in skin); transient; resolves in weeks.
  • Hepatosplenomegaly, hepatitis, jaundice.
  • Anaemia (haemolytic).
  • Meningoencephalitis — lethargy, irritability, seizures; chronic.
  • Microcephaly, intellectual disability, developmental delay, autism.
  • Radiolucent bone disease — metaphyseal lucencies (long bones).
  • Pneumonitis, interstitial lung disease.
  • Endocrine disorders — diabetes mellitus (Type 1, late onset — due to pancreatic insufficiency); thyroiditis, hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency.
  • Progressive rubella panencephalitis (PRP) — rare; late-onset neurodegenerative disorder (2nd decade); fatal.

Diagnosis

1. Maternal Diagnosis

  • Serology:
    • Rubella-specific IgM — indicates recent infection (persists 1–3 months).
    • Rubella-specific IgG avidity — low avidity suggests recent infection (<3 months); high avidity = past infection.
    • Four-fold rise in IgG titre between paired sera (acute & convalescent).
  • RT-PCR — detect rubella RNA in maternal throat, urine, blood.
  • Clinical — maternal rash, lymphadenopathy, arthralgia; often subclinical.

2. Prenatal Diagnosis

  • RT-PCR on amniotic fluid or fetal blood (after 18–22 weeks).
  • Fetal blood — rubella-specific IgM (after 22 weeks when fetal immune system is mature).
  • Ultrasound — IUGR, cardiac defects, microcephaly, echogenic bowel.
  • Chorionic villus sampling — PCR.

3. Postnatal Diagnosis of Newborn

  • Rubella-specific IgM in neonatal blood — indicates congenital infection (IgM does not cross placenta; produced by fetus). Persists 6–12 months.
  • Rubella-specific IgG — persists at high titre beyond 6–12 months (maternal IgG wanes by 6 months); high IgG in infant at 6 months suggests congenital infection.
  • RT-PCR / viral culture — throat swab, urine, CSF, rectal swab, lens aspirate (cataract); virus shed for months.
  • Complete blood count — thrombocytopenia, anaemia.
  • Liver function tests — elevated transaminases.
  • Audiology evaluation — brainstem auditory evoked potentials (BAER); often missed at birth; assess serially.
  • Ophthalmologic examination — cataract, glaucoma, retinopathy.
  • Echocardiography — PDA, pulmonary stenosis, VSD.
  • Ultrasound brain — calcifications, ventriculomegaly.
  • X-ray long bones — metaphyseal lucencies.

Differential Diagnosis — Other TORCH Infections

  • T — Toxoplasma gondii — chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications (periventricular).
  • O — Other — Syphilis, VZV, Parvovirus B19, Listeria.
  • R — Rubella — cataract, PDA, deafness.
  • C — Cytomegalovirus (CMV) — petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, sensorineural hearing loss, periventricular calcifications, microcephaly.
  • H — Herpes simplex virus (HSV) — vesicular skin lesions, encephalitis, hepatitis.

Treatment

  • No specific antiviral therapy.
  • Supportive:
    • Cataract — surgery (lensectomy, IOL implantation).
    • Glaucoma — surgical.
    • Cardiac defects — surgical correction (PDA ligation, pulmonary valvotomy).
    • Hearing aids, cochlear implant.
    • Developmental intervention — physiotherapy, speech therapy, special education.
    • Thrombocytopenia — IVIG if severe.
    • Diabetes — insulin.
  • Isolation — infant sheds virus for months; droplet precautions in hospital.

Prevention

  • Rubella vaccine:
    • Live attenuated — RA 27/3 strain.
    • Given as MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) — at 12–15 months + booster at 4–6 years.
    • Or MR (measles-rubella) — used in India's UIP.
    • India's MR campaign (2017–2019) — mass vaccination of children 9 months–15 years.
  • Pre-pregnancy screening:
    • Check rubella IgG before conception.
    • If negative — vaccinate; avoid pregnancy for 1 month after vaccination.
  • Pregnancy:
    • Antenatal screening — rubella IgG at first antenatal visit.
    • If IgG negative — avoid exposure; vaccinate postpartum.
    • Live vaccine is CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy — theoretical risk to fetus; inadvertent vaccination is not indication for termination (no confirmed CRS cases from vaccine strain).
  • Post-exposure prophylaxis:
    • Immune globulin (IG) within 72 h of exposure — for exposed pregnant women who are seronegative; does not prevent infection but may reduce severity; not routinely recommended.
  • Public health:
    • Universal childhood immunisation — herd immunity.
    • Outbreak investigation.
    • Surveillance of CRS cases.

Clinical Pearl

The Gregg triad — cataract, cardiac defects (PDA), and deafness — is the classic presentation of CRS. Sir Norman Gregg, an Australian ophthalmologist, first described the association in 1941 after observing a cluster of congenital cataract cases following a rubella epidemic. Risk of CRS is highest in 1st trimester (90% at <4 weeks; 50% at 5–8 weeks) and drops sharply after 20 weeks. Sensorineural deafness is the most common manifestation and may be the only defect in late 2nd trimester infection — always include hearing assessment (BAER) in newborn screening for CRS. Thrombocytopenic purpura ("blueberry muffin baby") — extramedullary haematopoiesis in skin — is a transient but striking neonatal presentation. Diabetes mellitus (Type 1) may develop in adolescence as a late complication — due to gradual pancreatic β-cell destruction. Rubella vaccine is the most effective preventive intervention — India's MR campaign (2017–2019) targeted 410 million children; CRS incidence has dropped dramatically. Live rubella vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy but inadvertent vaccination is NOT an indication for termination (no confirmed CRS cases from RA 27/3 strain). Always check rubella IgG in pre-pregnancy counselling — vaccinate seronegative women before conception. CRS is now rare in countries with universal rubella vaccination but remains a problem in countries without routine vaccination.

Introduction

Two types of polio vaccine have been used globally — OPV (oral polio vaccine, Sabin) and IPV (inactivated polio vaccine, Salk). Together, they have brought polio to the brink of eradication. India was certified polio-free by WHO on 27 March 2014.

1. OPV — Oral Polio Vaccine (Sabin)

  • Type — live attenuated; trivalent (tOPV — types 1, 2, 3), bivalent (bOPV — types 1, 3), monovalent (mOPV1, mOPV2, mOPV3).
  • Strain — Sabin strains; attenuated by serial passage in monkey kidney cells & lower temperature.
  • Administration — oral; 2 drops.
  • Schedule (India):
    • Birth dose (zero dose) — within 15 days of birth.
    • Primary — 6, 10, 14 weeks.
    • Boosters — 16–18 months, 5 years.
    • Pulse polio — additional doses during NIDs/SNIDs.
  • Storage:
    • Long-term — frozen at –20 °C (3 years).
    • Short-term — +2 to +8 °C (6 months).
    • Vaccine vial monitor (VVM) — square inside circle; if square darker than circle, discard.

Advantages of OPV

  • Mucosal immunity (IgA) — prevents intestinal replication & transmission; interrupts wild poliovirus spread in community.
  • Herd immunity — vaccine virus spreads to contacts → vaccinates unimmunised; crucial for eradication.
  • Easy administration — oral (no needle); no trained personnel needed.
  • Low cost — ~3 cents/dose vs ~$5 for IPV.
  • Humoral immunity (IgG) — protects against paralytic polio.
  • Mass campaign suitability — NIDs feasible.

Disadvantages of OPV

  • Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Poliomyelitis (VAPP):
    • Rare — ~1 case per 2.4 million doses (first dose risk: 1 in 750,000).
    • Due to reversion of attenuated strain to neurovirulent form.
    • Affects vaccine recipient or close contact.
  • Circulating Vaccine-Derived Poliovirus (cVDPV):
    • When vaccine virus replicates in under-immunised population → reverts to neurovirulence → causes outbreaks.
    • Type 2 most common (cVDPV2) — led to global switch from tOPV to bOPV in April 2016.
    • Risk in areas with low OPV coverage.
  • Not effective in immunodeficient individuals — may establish chronic infection & shedding (iVDPV — immunodeficiency-related VDPV).
  • Cold chain dependent — heat-sensitive.
  • Interference — concurrent enterovirus infections reduce efficacy; requires multiple doses in tropics (~10 doses for full protection in India).

2. IPV — Inactivated Polio Vaccine (Salk)

  • Type — killed/inactivated; trivalent (types 1, 2, 3).
  • Strain — Salk (wild strains — Mahoney, MEF-1, Saukett) inactivated by formaldehyde.
  • Administration — intramuscular (deltoid — adults; anterolateral thigh — infants) or subcutaneous; 0.5 mL.
  • Schedule:
    • 3 doses at 6, 10, 14 weeks (with DPT — as part of pentavalent + IPV).
    • Booster at 16–18 months.
    • India introduced fractional IPV (fIPV — 1/5th dose intradermally) to stretch supply; 2 doses at 6 & 14 weeks.
  • Storage — +2 to +8 °C; no freezing.

Advantages of IPV

  • No risk of VAPP or cVDPV — killed virus cannot revert.
  • Safety in immunocompromised — can be given safely.
  • Excellent humoral immunity (IgG) — protects against paralytic polio.
  • No cold chain issues — more heat-stable than OPV.
  • Cannot cause vaccine-derived outbreaks.

Disadvantages of IPV

  • NO mucosal immunity (IgA) — does not prevent intestinal replication & transmission; vaccinated individuals can still carry & spread wild poliovirus.
  • Does NOT provide herd immunity — cannot interrupt transmission.
  • Injection — requires trained personnel; sterile technique; risk of needle-stick injury.
  • Higher cost — ~$5/dose vs OPV's $0.03.
  • Lower efficacy in developing countries — possible interference from concurrent enteroviruses.

Comparison: OPV vs IPV

TypeLive attenuatedKilled (inactivated)

Mucosal immunity (IgA)YesNo

India's Polio Eradication Strategy

  1. Routine immunisation — OPV at birth, 6, 10, 14 weeks, 16–18 months, 5 years.
  2. Pulse polio immunisation (NIDs/SNIDs) — 2 supplementary OPV doses to all <5 yr children on same day, 4–6 weeks apart.
  3. mOPV1 & bOPV — for targeted campaigns against specific serotypes.
  4. House-to-house "mop-up" rounds — in areas with cases or low coverage.
  5. Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) surveillance — report & investigate every case of AFP in <15 yr; 2 stool samples 24–48 h apart for poliovirus isolation.
  6. Environmental surveillance — sewage sampling for poliovirus.
  7. Migration points — transit booths at railway stations, bus stands; migrant population tracking.
  8. Introduction of IPV (2015) — alongside OPV; fractional IPV (fIPV) at 6 & 14 weeks.
  9. Switch from tOPV to bOPV (April 2016) — removed type 2 component (no wild type 2 since 1999; cVDPV2 risk from tOPV).
  10. Community engagement — religious leaders, community mobilisers; especially for Muslim communities in UP/Bihar (resistance due to rumours).

Polio Endgame Strategy (WHO)

  1. Switch from tOPV to bOPV (April 2016) — globally.
  2. Introduce IPV into routine immunisation — provides type 2 immunity.
  3. Phase out OPV — eventually withdraw bOPV when wild polio eradicated.
  4. Switch to all-IPV schedule — once cVDPV risk eliminated.
  5. Containment — destroy or securely store poliovirus stocks (laboratories, vaccine production).
  6. Post-eradication surveillance — environmental & AFP.

Clinical Pearl

India was certified polio-free by WHO on 27 March 2014 — 3 years after the last wild poliovirus case (13 January 2011, Howrah, West Bengal). This was achieved through massive pulse polio campaigns reaching >170 million children twice yearly, house-to-house mop-up rounds, transit booths at railway stations, mobile teams for migrant populations, and intense community engagement (especially religious leaders to address Muslim community resistance). The last case of wild poliovirus globally was in Pakistan/Afghanistan — the two remaining endemic countries. The global switch from tOPV to bOPV in April 2016 was a major milestone — type 2 was eradicated in 1999, and the type 2 component of OPV was causing most cVDPV outbreaks. India now uses bOPV + IPV in routine immunisation — IPV provides type 2 immunity (since bOPV lacks type 2). Fractional IPV (fIPV — 1/5th dose intradermally) at 6 & 14 weeks was introduced to stretch limited IPV supply — intradermal route induces equivalent immunity with 1/5th the dose. The future endgame is complete withdrawal of OPV (because of VAPP & cVDPV risks) and switch to all-IPV schedule, once wild poliovirus is eradicated globally & cVDPV outbreaks controlled. AFP surveillance remains the cornerstone — every case of acute flaccid paralysis in a child <15 yr must be reported within 14 days, with 2 stool samples collected 24–48 h apart for poliovirus isolation (reverse cold chain maintained).

Introduction

The physician's role in the healthcare system extends far beyond the traditional diagnosis-treatment model. A modern physician is a clinician, communicator, collaborator, health advocate, leader, scholar, and professional. The CanMEDS framework (Royal College of Physicians & Surgeons of Canada) and the Indian Medical Council's professional roles define these dimensions.

The Seven Roles of a Physician (CanMEDS Framework)

1. Medical Expert / Clinician

  • Diagnostician — accurate diagnosis using history, examination, investigations; clinical reasoning; differential diagnosis.
  • Treating physician — evidence-based therapy; pharmacological, surgical, procedural, psychological interventions.
  • Proceduralist — perform indicated medical procedures.
  • Patient assessor — assess urgency, severity, prognosis; triage decisions.
  • Continuous learning — keep up-to-date with medical advances; continuing medical education (CME).
  • Clinical decision-making — risk-benefit analysis; shared decision-making with patient.

2. Communicator

  • Doctor-patient communication — listen actively; explain diagnosis, treatment options, prognosis in language patient understands; obtain informed consent.
  • Breaking bad news — use SPIKES protocol (Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Empathy, Strategy).
  • Empathy & compassion — emotional support; build trust & therapeutic alliance.
  • Documentation — accurate medical records; medico-legal documentation.
  • Communication with family — involve family in decision-making (especially in Indian context where family is central).
  • Communication with colleagues & team — handovers, referrals, consultations.
  • Health education — patient & family counselling on disease, prevention, lifestyle.

3. Collaborator

  • Team-based care — work effectively in multidisciplinary teams (nurses, pharmacists, physiotherapists, social workers, dietitians, technicians).
  • Referrals & consultations — recognise limits of own expertise; refer appropriately; communicate effectively with specialists.
  • Inter-professional collaboration — respect roles of other healthcare professionals.
  • Coordinating care — across primary, secondary, tertiary levels; smooth transitions.
  • Family engagement — involve family in care planning & decision-making.

4. Leader / Manager

  • Healthcare leadership — lead clinical teams; allocate resources efficiently.
  • Quality improvement — participate in clinical audit; identify system errors; implement improvements.
  • Patient safety — report errors & near-misses; implement safety protocols.
  • Resource stewardship — judicious use of investigations & treatments; cost-conscious care.
  • Administration — manage clinics, wards, hospitals; participate in hospital committees.
  • Health policy — contribute to local, regional, national health policy development.

5. Health Advocate

  • Individual advocacy — advocate for individual patient's needs (access to care, social support, insurance).
  • Community advocacy — promote public health; disease prevention; vaccination; healthy lifestyle.
  • Social determinants of health — address poverty, education, housing, sanitation; understand & act on social determinants.
  • Health equity — work to reduce disparities in access & outcomes for vulnerable populations (poor, rural, women, children, elderly, marginalised).
  • Public health emergencies — respond to outbreaks, disasters; disease surveillance & reporting.

Sir William Osler's aphorism: "The good physician treats the disease; the great physician treats the patient who has the disease." Introduction

Naegleria fowleri — "brain-eating amoeba" — is a free-living amoeba found in warm freshwater (lakes, ponds, hot springs, untreated swimming pools, warm industrial discharge, soil). It causes Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis (PAM) — a rare (annual global incidence <300 cases) but >97% fatal disease. First described by Fowler & Carter (1965) in Australia.

Life Cycle

Naegleria fowleri exists in three forms — trophozoite, flagellate, and cyst.

1. Trophozoite (Infective & Reproductive Form)

  • Morphology — 10–25 µm; elongated or amoeboid; single nucleus with prominent central nucleolus; contractile vacuole; blunt pseudopodia (lobopodia).
  • Reproduction — binary fission; every 8 h under optimal conditions.
  • Feeding — phagocytoses bacteria, yeast, organic debris.
  • Motility — active pseudopodial movement.
  • Optimal temperature — 37–45 °C (thermophilic; survives up to 46 °C).
  • Pathogenic form — causes PAM.

2. Flagellate Form (Temporary — for Dispersal)

  • Morphology — pear-shaped; 2 flagella at broad end; swims rapidly.
  • Transformation — trophozoite converts to flagellate when ionic balance changes (e.g., placed in distilled water); reverts to trophozoite when conditions improve (within hours).
  • Function — allows dispersal through water in search of food; not feeding; not dividing.
  • NOT infective.

3. Cyst Form (Dormant — for Survival)

  • Morphology — 7–15 µm; spherical; thick double wall; single nucleus; pores for excystation.
  • Formation — trophozoite encysts under unfavourable conditions (cold, desiccation, food depletion, low nutrient).
  • Survival — resistant to cold (survives months at 4 °C), drying, chlorine (tolerates low levels); NOT resistant to boiling.
  • Cysts are NOT formed in human tissue — only in environment.

Life Cycle Stages

  1. In environment — trophozoites multiply in warm freshwater (lakes, ponds, hot springs, swimming pools, soil, warm industrial discharge). When conditions become unfavourable, trophozoites encyst.
  2. Entry into human host — when contaminated water enters nose (swimming, diving, water sports, nasal irrigation with neti pot using tap water, ritual ablution), trophozoites are forced into nasal passages.
  3. Penetration of nasal mucosa — trophozoites attach to olfactory epithelium using food cups (amebostomes) & surface glycoproteins.
  4. Migration along olfactory nerve — through cribriform plate of ethmoid bone into olfactory bulb (subarachnoid space); short distance (~1 cm); bypasses blood-brain barrier.
  5. Invasion of brain — trophozoites multiply in brain tissue (meninges, cortex, basal ganglia); phagocytose brain tissue (esp. red blood cells, neurons); release cytotoxic enzymes (phospholipases, proteases, neuraminidases).
  6. Haematogenous spread — rare; trophozoites may spread systemically but PAM is primarily a CNS infection.
  7. No cyst formation in human tissue — only trophozoites found in brain.
  8. Transmission — human-to-human does NOT occur; no person-to-person spread.

Pathogenicity — Mechanisms

1. Pore-Forming Proteins (Naegleriapores)

  • Trophozoites release naegleriapores A & B — pore-forming peptides that create holes in target cell membranes → cell lysis & death.
  • Effective against bacteria, RBCs, neurons.

2. Cytopathic Enzymes

  • Phospholipase A2 & phospholipase B — degrade membrane phospholipids → cell lysis.
  • Proteases — elastase, collagenase, trypsin-like; degrade extracellular matrix & facilitate tissue invasion.
  • Neuraminidase — cleaves sialic acid from cell surfaces.
  • Elastase — degrades elastin in vessel walls.

3. Phagocytosis (Amebostome)

  • Trophozoites form food cups (amebostomes) — specialised structures for ingesting brain tissue (RBCs, neurons, myelin).
  • Phagocytosed tissue digested in phagolysosomes.

4. Adhesion Molecules

  • Surface glycoproteins (Nfa1 protein) — mediate attachment to olfactory epithelium & brain cells.
  • Integrin-like molecules.

5. Immune Evasion

  • Complement resistance — N. fowleri expresses complement regulatory proteins; resists complement-mediated lysis.
  • Antigenic variation.
  • Resistance to neutrophil oxidative killing.
  • Phagocytosis of immune cells.

6. Inflammatory Response

  • Purulent meningitis — neutrophilic infiltrate in meninges & brain tissue; haemorrhagic necrosis of olfactory bulb & frontal cortex.
  • Granulomas absent (unlike Acanthamoeba).

Clinical Features — PAM (Primary Amoebic Meningoencephalitis)

  • Incubation — 1–9 days (usually 2–5 days) after water exposure.
  • Stage 1 (Prodrome, 1–3 days):
    • Severe bifrontal/bitemporal headache.
    • Fever (often high — 38.5–40 °C).
    • Nausea, vomiting.
    • Altered smell (anosmia) & taste (ageusia) — due to olfactory nerve involvement.
    • Sore throat, rhinitis.
  • Stage 2 (Meningoencephalitis, 3–7 days):
    • Stiff neck (meningismus).
    • Photophobia.
    • Altered mental status — confusion, lethargy, delirium.
    • Seizures (focal or generalised).
    • Cranial nerve palsies (especially III, IV, VI).
    • Cerebellar ataxia.
    • Coma.
  • Death — typically within 3–7 days of symptom onset; case fatality rate >97% (only ~7 survivors reported globally as of 2023).

Laboratory Diagnosis

1. CSF Analysis

  • Lumbar puncture — CSF shows features of acute bacterial meningitis but culture negative for bacteria:
    • Opening pressure — elevated (>20 cm H₂O).
    • WBC — markedly elevated (500–25,000/µL); neutrophilic predominant.
    • RBC — elevated (haemorrhagic).
    • Glucose — decreased (<40 mg/dL).
    • Protein — elevated (100–500 mg/dL).
    • Gram stain — negative (no bacteria); may show motile trophozoites.
  • Wet mount of CSF — examine under microscope immediately (warm stage 37 °C); motile trophozoites seen within minutes; characteristic rapid locomotion (eruptive pseudopodia).
  • Phase contrast or DIC microscopy — better visualisation.
  • Trichrome stain, Giemsa, Wright's stain — trophozoites have single nucleus with large central nucleolus.
  • Calcofluor white — for cysts (if present).

2. Culture

  • Culture on non-nutrient agar seeded with E. coli or Enterobacter — 37–42 °C; trophozoites feed on bacteria & form plaques; multiply.
  • Enflagellation test — place CSF sediment in distilled water; trophozoites transform into pear-shaped flagellates within 1–2 h — confirms N. fowleri (distinguishes from Acanthamoeba which does not form flagellates).

3. Molecular Tests

  • PCR — detects N. fowleri DNA in CSF, brain tissue, environmental water; target genes (Mp2Cl5, internal transcribed spacer, 18S rRNA); specific & sensitive.
  • Real-time PCR — quantitative; rapid.
  • Immunofluorescence — direct fluorescent antibody test on CSF or tissue.

4. Other Tests

  • CT head — may show cerebral oedema, obliterated cisterns, hydrocephalus; usually unremarkable early.
  • MRI — leptomeningeal enhancement; cerebral oedema; olfactory bulb involvement.
  • Blood tests — leucocytosis, neutrophilia.
  • Brain biopsy — trophozoites in tissue; postmortem.

Differential Diagnosis

  • Acute bacterial meningitis — negative bacterial culture suggests PAM; CSF wet mount for amoeba is diagnostic.
  • Herpes simplex encephalitis — temporal lobe involvement; PCR positive for HSV.
  • Acanthamoeba meningoencephalitis (GAE) — chronic; immunocompromised; cysts in tissue; no flagellate form.
  • Balamuthia mandrillaris — chronic; granulomatous; skin lesion often present.

Treatment

  • Combination therapy — no proven regimen; based on case reports of survivors.
    • Amphotericin B IV (1.5 mg/kg/day) — mainstay; crosses BBB; also intrathecal/intraventricular.
    • Miltefosine (oral; 50 mg BD × 28 days) — newer; anti-amoebic; also used for leishmaniasis.
    • Fluconazole or ketoconazole.
    • Rifampicin.
    • Azithromycin.
    • Sulfadiazine.
  • Supportive care — ICU; mechanical ventilation; control raised ICP (mannitol, hypertonic saline, hyperventilation); anticonvulsants; control fever.
  • Hypothermia — induced hypothermia has been used in survivors (reduce brain oedema).
  • Despite treatment, mortality >97%.

Prevention

  • Avoid swimming in warm freshwater (lakes, ponds, hot springs) — especially during summer; particularly in southern US, Australia, India.
  • Use nose clips while swimming; keep head above water.
  • Avoid digging in sediment of warm freshwater.
  • Use only boiled, filtered, or distilled water for nasal irrigation (neti pot, ritual ablution); tap water may contain amoebae.
  • Proper chlorination of swimming pools (≥1 ppm free chlorine); maintenance of pool filters.
  • Avoid untreated warm water in cooling towers, industrial discharge.
  • Education — awareness of risk; seek immediate medical attention for severe headache & fever after freshwater exposure.

Clinical Pearl

The key clue to PAM is recent freshwater exposure (1–9 days) with acute onset of severe headache, fever, & meningeal signs in an otherwise healthy child or young adult. CSF shows features of acute bacterial meningitis but Gram stain is negative & culture is sterile — always do a wet mount of fresh warm CSF to look for motile trophozoites — the amoebae move rapidly with eruptive pseudopodia; characteristic appearance is diagnostic. The enflagellation test (distilled water) confirms — N. fowleri transforms into pear-shaped flagellate form (Acanthamoeba does not). Mortality is >97% — most patients die within 3–7 days of symptom onset. Always suspect PAM in any febrile patient with meningeal signs & recent freshwater exposure — early diagnosis & aggressive combination therapy (amphotericin B + miltefosine + fluconazole + rifampicin + azithromycin + sulfadiazine) is the only chance of survival. The most important preventive advice — avoid warm freshwater swimming; use nose clips; use only boiled/distilled water for nasal irrigation. PAM cases in India have been reported from warm freshwater sources in summer; awareness is critical. The CDC offers free miltefosine for PAM treatment through investigational new drug (IND) protocol — contact CDC immediately if PAM suspected.

Urethritis is inflammation of the urethra, presenting with urethral discharge & dysuria. Classified as gonococcal urethritis (GU — caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae) & non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU — caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma urealyticum, Trichomonas vaginalis, HSV, and others).   • Systemic — fever, rash, joint pain (disseminated gonococcal infection).

    • Thayer-Martin for N. gonorrhoeae (also gives antimicrobial susceptibility).

  • Partner notification & treatment.
  • Expedited partner therapy (EPT) — patient delivers prescription to partner without clinician visit (where legal).
  • Health education.
  • Vaccines — HPV (Gardasil 9); HBV; no vaccine for N. gonorrhoeae (candidates in trials; outer membrane vesicle — MeNZB showed cross-protection).

The single most useful bedside test is Gram stain of urethral discharge — intracellular Gram-negative diplococci in polymorphs = gonococcal urethritis. Pregnant women — screen & treat; ceftriaxone safe; azithromycin safe; avoid doxycycline. Ophthalmia neonatorum prophylaxis — 0.5% erythromycin or 1% tetracycline eye ointment at birth; also prevents chlamydial conjunctivitis. India's STI/RTI control programme (NACP) uses syndromic management — treat all urethritis with ceftriaxone + azithromycin; covers both organisms.

Introduction

Plague is an acute zoonotic bacterial infection caused by Yersinia pestis — a Gram-negative, non-motile, facultatively anaerobic, pleomorphic coccobacillus of family Enterobacteriaceae. Primarily a disease of rodents (enzootic cycle — rats, prairie dogs, squirrels); transmitted to humans by flea bite (Xenopsylla cheopis — rat flea). Plague caused 3 historic pandemics (Justinian, Black Death, modern); millions of deaths.

Transmission

  • Flea bite — primary route; rat flea (Xenopsylla cheopis) regurgitates Y. pestis into bite wound after blood meal (blockage of flea proventriculus by biofilm → bacillus multiplication → regurgitation).
  • Direct contact with infected animal tissue (hunting, skinning rabbits, prairie dogs).
  • Inhalation of respiratory droplets — from pneumonic plague patient or animal (rare but highly contagious).
  • Incubation — 2–8 days for bubonic; 1–3 days for pneumonic.
  • Bioterrorism — Category A agent (aerosol dissemination).

Clinical Types

1. Bubonic Plague — Most Common (80–95% of cases)

  • Incubation — 2–8 days after flea bite.
  • Onset — sudden high fever (39–40 °C), chills, severe malaise, headache, myalgia.
  • Bubo:
    • Swollen, extremely tender lymph node(s) draining the flea bite site.
    • Usually inguinal (most common — flea bites legs); also axillary, cervical (depending on bite site).
    • 1–10 cm; oval, firm, fixed to surrounding tissue; overlying skin erythematous, warm, oedematous; may suppurate & drain.
    • Severe pain — patient guards affected area; refuses to move limb.
  • Systemic — tachycardia, hypotension, altered mental state (toxic, delirious).
  • Skin — flea bite site may show papule, pustule, eschar; purpura, petechiae.
  • Without treatment — progresses to septicaemic plague in 50–80%; mortality 60–100%.
  • With prompt antibiotics — mortality 5–15%.

2. Septicaemic Plague (10–15% of cases)

  • Can occur as primary (no bubo) or secondary to bubonic.
  • Primary septicaemic — Y. pestis enters bloodstream directly without lymph node involvement; seen in older patients & immunocompromised.
  • Features:
    • High fever, chills, profound prostration, hypotension, shock.
    • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) — petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses; bleeding from mucous membranes; gangrene of extremities (acral — fingers, toes, nose) — "Black Death" appearance.
    • Multi-organ failure — ARDS, AKI, hepatic failure, meningitis.
    • No bubo (or very small, overlooked).
  • Mortality — 30–50% even with treatment; near 100% untreated.

3. Pneumonic Plague — Most Severe, Highly Contagious

  • Secondary pneumonic — complication of bubonic/septicaemic plague (~5%); haematogenous spread to lungs.
  • Primary pneumonic — inhalation of respiratory droplets from pneumonic plague patient or infected animal; bioterrorism risk.
  • Incubation — 1–3 days (shortest).
  • Features:
    • Sudden high fever, chills, severe headache, malaise.
    • Productive cough with bloody, watery, purulent sputum ("watery tomato soup").
    • Dyspnoea, tachypnoea, chest pain, cyanosis.
    • Bilateral consolidation; ARDS.
    • Rapid progression — septic shock, multi-organ failure, death within 24–48 h.
  • Highly contagious — person-to-person via respiratory droplets; close contact required.
  • Mortality — >90% even with treatment; 100% untreated (within 24–48 h).
  • Quarantine & isolation required.

4. Meningeal Plague (Rare — <1%)

  • Complication of any form (especially in children); haematogenous spread to meninges.
  • Features — fever, headache, neck stiffness, altered mental status, seizures.
  • CSF — purulent; Gram-negative coccobacilli on stain.
  • Treatment — IV chloramphenicol (drug of choice for plague meningitis) + streptomycin/gentamicin.

5. Pharyngeal Plague

  • Rare; from ingestion of contaminated food or inhalation.
  • Features — sore throat, fever, cervical lymphadenitis; mimics pharyngitis/tonsillitis.
  • May be confused with diphtheria.

6. Cutaneous Plague

  • Rare; pustule, eschar, ulcer at flea bite site; cellulitis; purpura.

Pathogenesis

  • Y. pestis virulence factors:
    • F1 capsule (Fraction 1 antigen) — anti-phagocytic; only expressed at 37 °C.
    • V & W antigens — anti-phagocytic; virulence determinant.
    • Yops (Yersinia outer membrane proteins) — YopH (dephosphorylates macrophage signalling → inhibits phagocytosis); YopE, YopM, YopJ — various immune evasion.
    • Pla (plasminogen activator protease) — degrades fibrin, extracellular matrix → spreads; haematogenous dissemination.
    • Pst (pesticin) — iron acquisition.
    • Endotoxin (LPS) — septic shock.
    • Type III secretion system (injectosome) — injects Yops into host cells.
  • Phases:
    1. Flea bite → Y. pestis enters skin.
    2. Phagocytosed by neutrophils & macrophages — but resists killing (F1 capsule, Yops); multiplies intracellularly in macrophages.
    3. Macrophages carry Y. pestis to regional lymph node.
    4. Y. pestis escapes macrophage, multiplies extracellularly → intense inflammation → bubo.
    5. May enter bloodstream → septicaemia → DIC, multi-organ failure.
    6. May spread to lungs → pneumonic plague → contagious via droplets.

Diagnosis

  • Specimen:
    • Bubo aspirate (saline injected into bubo & aspirated).
    • Blood culture (septicaemic).
    • Sputum, throat swab (pneumonic).
    • CSF (meningeal).
  • Gram stain & Wayson stain — Gram-negative coccobacilli (bipolar staining — "closed safety pin" appearance with Wayson's or Giemsa).
  • Culture:
    • Blood agar, MacConkey agar — slow-growing (24–48 h).

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) — family Herpesviridae, subfamily Alphaherpesvirinae, genus Simplexvirus — is a dsDNA virus causing mucocutaneous, genital, ocular, and CNS infections.   • Vesicle fluid / swab from lesion base — unroof vesicle; swab base (cells for direct fluorescent antibody & PCR); vesicle fluid for culture.
  • Genital swab — urethral, cervical, vaginal, anal.
  • CSF — for HSV encephalitis.
  • Corneal scrapings — for HSV keratitis.
  • Blood (EDTA) — for disseminated HSV; PCR.
  • Saliva / throat swab — for primary oral HSV; gingivostomatitis.
  • Transport — viral transport medium (Stuart's, HBSS); refrigerate (4 °C); process within 24 h; freeze at –70 °C if longer delay.

2. Direct Microscopy

  • Tzanck smear:
    • Scrape base of unroofed vesicle; smear on slide; stain with Giemsa, Wright, or Papanicolaou.
    • Multinucleated giant cells with moulded nuclei; eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions (Cowdry type A bodies) — characteristic of HSV & VZV (not specific for HSV).
    • Rapid; sensitivity 40–60%.
  • Direct Fluorescent Antibody (DFA):
    • Smear fixed with acetone; stained with fluorescent-labelled anti-HSV-1 & anti-HSV-2 monoclonal antibodies.
    • Apple-green fluorescence under UV microscope.
    • Sensitivity 70–90%; specificity >95%.
    • Distinguishes HSV-1 from HSV-2.
  • Electron microscopy:
    • Direct visualisation of viral particles in vesicle fluid.
    • Hexagonal capsid with envelope (typical herpesvirus morphology).
    • Cannot distinguish HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV.
    • Research use; not routine.

3. Viral Culture

  • Cell lines:
    • Vero cells (African green monkey kidney) — most common.
    • MRC-5, WI-38 (human diploid fibroblasts) — sensitive for HSV.
    • BSC-1, HEp-2, RK-13.
    • Shell vial culture — centrifugation-enhanced; faster.
  • Cytopathic effect (CPE):
    • Appears in 1–7 days (often 24–48 h).
    • Balloon degeneration — rounded, refractile cells.
    • Synctia formation — multinucleated giant cells.
    • Focal & spreading — plaques.
  • Confirmation:
    • DFA on infected cells — distinguishes HSV-1 from HSV-2.
    • Neutralisation with specific antisera.
    • PCR for typing.
  • Sensitivity — high for vesicular lesion (90%); lower for ulcer (70%); low for crusted lesion (30%); low for recurrent (viral load lower). Culture is being replaced by PCR — more sensitive & faster.

  • PCR targets — glycoprotein B (gB), gD, DNA polymerase (UL30), thymidine kinase (UL23); type-specific primers for HSV-1 & HSV-2.
  • Specimens — vesicle swab, genital swab, CSF, blood, corneal scrapings, saliva.
  • Advantages:
    • High sensitivity (95%+) & specificity.
    • Rapid (4–24 h).
    • Detects non-viable virus (after lesion has crusted).
    • Type-specific (HSV-1 vs HSV-2).
    • Quantitative (viral load).
  • Real-time PCR — quantitative; faster; multiplex with VZV.
  • CSF PCR — test of choice for HSV encephalitis (sensitivity 95–98% in first week; specificity 95–99%).
  • Multiplex PCR panels — BioFire FilmArray Meningitis/Encephalitis panel (HSV-1, HSV-2 + others in 1 hour).

    • Uses type-specific glycoprotein G (gG1 for HSV-1; gG2 for HSV-2) — distinguishes the two types.

    • Methods — ELISA, immunoblot, chemiluminescence.
  • Uses:
    • Epidemiological surveys (prevalence).
    • Identify asymptomatic HSV-2 carriers (counselling).
    • Screen pregnant women (prevent neonatal herpes).
    • Determine susceptible sexual partners.
  • Limitations:
    • Cannot distinguish primary from recurrent infection (IgM unreliable).
    • Cannot identify active shedding site (oral vs genital).
    • Serology cannot replace PCR/culture for acute mucocutaneous disease.

    • Complement fixation, neutralisation — cannot distinguish HSV-1 from HSV-2; cross-react.
    • Now obsolete.

  • Skin biopsy — intraepidermal vesicle; acantholytic cells; multinucleated giant cells with moulded nuclei; eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions (Cowdry type A); balloon degeneration of keratinocytes.
  • Brain biopsy (HSV encephalitis):
    • Historical gold standard (now PCR preferred — less invasive).

  • Corneal scrape (HSV keratitis):

    • Slit-lamp examination diagnostic.

  • Brush biopsy / Pap smear — cytology may show HSV inclusions.
  • CSF analysis (HSV encephalitis):

    • PCR positive for HSV DNA.
  • MRI brain (HSV encephalitis):
    • Temporal lobe (medial) T2/FLAIR hyperintensity; often bilateral asymmetric.
    • Early — diffusion restriction (DWI).
    • Later — haemorrhage, necrosis, atrophy.
    • More sensitive than CT (especially early).

  • Slit-lamp examination (eye) — dendritic corneal ulcer; classic for HSV keratitis.

Recurrent mucocutaneous lesionPCR (more sensitive than culture in recurrent disease)
HSV encephalitisCSF PCR (gold standard; sensitivity 95–98%)

Mycetoma (Madura foot) is a chronic, progressive, granulomatous subcutaneous infection characterised by the triad of tumefaction (swelling), formation of sinus tracts, & discharge of grains (colonies of the causative organism).   • Eumycetoma (fungal) — ~40% of cases; caused by true fungi.
  • Actinomycetoma (bacterial) — ~60% of cases; caused by filamentous bacteria (actinomycetes).

  • Risk groups — rural agricultural workers, farmers, herdsmen, labourers; males 3–5× more common (occupational exposure); ages 20–50 yr.
  • Endemic regions — India (Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan, Gujarat, West Bengal), Sudan, Mexico, Venezuela, Senegal, Somalia.
  • Incubation — months to years; very slow progression.

Clinical Features

  • Site — foot (70%); hand, leg, arm, back, neck, head also involved.
  • Initial lesion — painless subcutaneous nodule at site of trauma.
  • Progression:
    • Nodule enlarges; becomes fluctuant; ruptures to form sinus tract.
    • Multiple nodules & sinuses develop over months–years; discharge serosanguineous or purulent fluid containing grains (colonies of organism).
    • Subcutaneous tissue & skin become indurated, swollen, & deformed ("Madura foot").
    • Deeper structures involved — muscle, tendon, bone (osteomyelitis), joint; deformity, disability.
    • Lymphatic spread rare; haematogenous spread rare.
    • Usually painless until bone/joint involvement or secondary bacterial infection.
    • Slowly progressive over years; may cause severe disability but rarely fatal.
  • Grains — 0.5–2 mm; visible to naked eye; white, yellow, black, or red depending on organism.

Laboratory Diagnosis

1. Clinical Specimen

  • Grains from sinus discharge — collect on sterile gauze or in sterile saline; wash grains (remove blood/debris).
  • Pus from deep sinus — express & collect.
  • Tissue biopsy — deep lesion; full-thickness including subcutaneous tissue & bone if involved.
  • Needle aspirate from closed lesion.

2. Direct Microscopy

  • KOH mount of grains — examine grain morphology:
    • Eumycetoma — grain consists of septate hyphae (3–5 µm diameter) with chlamydospores; embedded in brown cement-like matrix; black or white grains.
    • Actinomycetoma — grain consists of fine filaments (1 µm diameter) (actinomycetes — narrower than fungal hyphae); white, yellow, or red grains.
  • Gram stain — actinomycetoma: Gram-positive branching filaments; eumycetoma: Gram-positive broader hyphae.
  • Modified acid-fast stain — Nocardia species are weakly acid-fast (partially retain carbol fuchsin with weak acid decolouriser); useful for differentiating actinomycetoma.
  • India ink — may help visualise capsule in some fungi.

3. Culture

  • For eumycetoma (fungi):
    • Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) with antibiotics (chloramphenicol, gentamicin) — inhibit bacteria; without cycloheximide (inhibits some fungi).
    • Incubate at 25–30 °C for 4–6 weeks (slow growth).
    • Identify by colony morphology, microscopy (lactophenol cotton blue mount), sugar assimilation, PCR.
  • For actinomycetoma (actinomycetes):
    • Sabouraud dextrose agar, Brain heart infusion agar, Blood agar, Lowenstein-Jensen.
    • Incubate at 37 °C for 2–4 weeks (aerobic).
    • Nocardia — weakly acid-fast, branching filaments; colonies chalky, powdery, earthy odour; urease positive; catalase positive.
    • Streptomyces, Actinomadura — similar techniques.
  • Culture is essential — identifies organism & guides therapy (eumycetoma vs actinomycetoma).

  • Skin/subcutaneous biopsy:
    • Granulomatous inflammation — epithelioid cells, giant cells, neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells.

    • Eumycetoma grains — septate hyphae in matrix (PAS, GMS stain positive).
    • Actinomycetoma grains — fine filaments (Gram-positive; weakly acid-fast; GMS positive).
  • Bone biopsy — if bone involvement; osteomyelitis changes.

    • Bone involvement — lytic lesions with sclerotic margins (cavitation); periosteal reaction; cortical destruction; "sun-ray" appearance (spicules perpendicular to cortex).

  • MRI:
    • Better soft tissue & bone detail.
    • "Dot-in-circle" sign — small hypointense foci (grains) within larger lesions; highly specific for mycetoma.

  • Ultrasound — may identify grains.
  • CT — for bone destruction.

  • PCR — identifies organism at species level; targets 18S rRNA, ITS region; useful for fastidious organisms; not widely available.
  • Real-time PCR — rapid; quantitative.
  • Sequencing — gold standard for species identification in reference labs.

7. Serology

  • ELISA, immunodiffusion — for antibodies; useful for follow-up & epidemiology; not widely available.
  • Antigen detection — experimental.

  • Actinomycosis — caused by Actinomyces israelii (endogenous); cervicofacial, thoracic, abdominal; discharge "sulphur granules" (yellowish, bacteria not fungi); not from traumatic inoculation.
  • Botryomycosis — bacterial (S. aureus, Pseudomonas); grains are bacterial aggregates; similar clinical appearance.
  • Chromoblastomycosis — fungal; sclerotic bodies ("copper pennies") in tissue; not grains.
  • Sporotrichosis — fungal; lymphocutaneous spread; no grains.
  • Tuberculosis (scrofuloderma) — caseating granuloma; AFB positive; no grains.
  • Leishmaniasis (cutaneous) — amastigotes in macrophages.
  • Kaposi sarcoma — vascular tumour; no grains.
  • Squamous cell carcinoma — Marjolin ulcer; biopsy diagnostic.

Eumycetoma (Fungal) — Difficult to Treat

  • Itraconazole 200–400 mg/day for 6–12 months (or longer) — drug of choice.
  • Terbinafine 500–1000 mg/day — alternative.
  • Voriconazole, posaconazole — newer azoles.
  • Amphotericin B IV — for severe or refractory cases; then maintenance azole.
  • Surgical excision — for localised lesions; combined with antifungals; amputation in advanced disease.
  • Outcome — cure rate 25–35%; high recurrence; long-term therapy needed.
  • Fosravuconazole — newer long-acting azole; in trials.

Actinomycetoma (Bacterial) — Better Response

  • Welsh regimen:
    • Streptomycin 1 g IM daily for 4 weeks + Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole) 960 mg BD for 12 months.
