  • Dapsone 100 mg/day — alternative (avoid in G6PD deficiency).
  • Minocycline, doxycycline — alternatives.
  • Linezolid, carbapenems — for resistant strains.
  • Surgical excision — for localised lesions.
  • Outcome — cure rate 60–90%; better than eumycetoma.

  • Wear shoes — most important; prevents traumatic inoculation.
  • Avoid barefoot walking in endemic areas.
  • Use protective gloves when handling soil/plant material.
  • Wound care for minor injuries.
  • Health education in endemic areas.
  • Early diagnosis & treatment — prevents progression to bone involvement & disability.

The classic triad of mycetoma — tumefaction (swelling), sinus tracts, & grains (colonies of organism) — is diagnostic. Introduction

Measles (Rubeola) is a highly contagious acute viral exanthem caused by Measles virus — an enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA virus of family Paramyxoviridae, genus Morbillivirus. Humans are the only natural host. Despite availability of effective vaccine, measles remains a leading cause of vaccine-preventable child mortality (~140,000 deaths globally in 2018; India accounts for ~10%).

Pathogenesis

1. Transmission

  • Airborne — respiratory droplets (cough, sneeze); highly contagious (R₀ = 12–18 — most contagious human virus).
  • Direct contact with nasal or throat secretions.
  • Fomites — virus survives 2 hours on surfaces.
  • Incubation — 8–12 days (range 7–21 days); infectivity from 4 days before rash to 4 days after.
  • Infective dose — very low; ~90% of susceptible contacts develop disease.

2. Viral Entry & Replication

  1. Entry via respiratory tract — virus inhaled; infects respiratory epithelial cells & lymphoid tissue (adenoids, tonsils).
  2. Receptor — Signalling Lymphocyte Activation Molecule (SLAM / CD150) on immune cells (T, B, dendritic, memory cells); also nectin-4 (Poliovirus receptor-like 4) on epithelial cells.
  3. Primary replication — respiratory epithelium & regional lymph nodes; 2–3 days.
  4. Primary viraemia — day 2–5; virus spreads to regional lymph nodes (cervical, mediastinal) & reticuloendothelial system (liver, spleen, thymus, bone marrow).
  5. Replication in lymphoid tissue — virus multiplies in T & B lymphocytes, dendritic cells; causes lymphopenia & immunosuppression (lasts weeks–months — basis for secondary bacterial infections & reactivation of TB).
  6. Secondary viraemia — day 5–7; virus spreads to skin, conjunctiva, respiratory tract, GI tract, kidneys, bladder.
  7. Rash — day 14 (after incubation); immune-mediated (cytotoxic T cells attack virus-infected endothelial cells in skin capillaries); appearance of rash coincides with antibody production & cessation of viraemia.

3. Mechanism of Rash

  • Measles rash is a Type IV hypersensitivity reaction — cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes recognise viral antigen on infected endothelial cells in dermis → cell-mediated cytotoxicity → rash.
  • Children with cellular immunodeficiency (e.g., leukaemia, HIV) do NOT develop typical rash — may develop giant cell pneumonia without rash.
  • Children with humoral immunodeficiency (e.g., agammaglobulinaemia) develop normal rash — cell-mediated immunity is intact.

4. Pathology

  • Warthin-Finkeldey giant cells — multinucleated giant cells with inclusion bodies in cytoplasm & nucleus; found in lymphoid tissue, respiratory epithelium, skin; pathognomonic for measles.
  • Interstitial pneumonia — giant cell pneumonia; especially in immunocompromised.
  • Koplik spots — pathognomonic grayish-white papules on buccal mucosa opposite lower molars; appear 1–2 days before rash; represent foci of viral replication & inflammation.

5. Immune Suppression

  • Measles-induced immunosuppression — profound; lasts weeks to months.
  • Mechanism:
    • Lymphocyte infection & depletion (lymphopenia).
    • Impaired T cell proliferation (IL-12 suppression).
    • Skewing of cytokine response from Th1 to Th2.
    • Delayed-type hypersensitivity suppression (anergy; tuberculin test becomes negative during & after measles — "measles anergy").
    • Dendritic cell dysfunction.
  • Consequences:
    • Secondary bacterial infections — pneumonia (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, S. aureus); otitis media; diarrhoea.
    • Reactivation of TB — quiescent TB may flare after measles.
    • Weight loss, malnutrition — worsens with measles.
    • Increased mortality — especially in malnourished children.

Clinical Features

  • Prodrome (3–5 days before rash):
    • Fever (39–40 °C); cough, coryza (runny nose), conjunctivitis — "3 Cs".
    • Malaise, anorexia, photophobia.
    • Koplik spots — pathognomonic; grayish-white papules on erythematous base on buccal mucosa opposite lower molars; appear 1–2 days before rash; disappear after rash appears.
  • Rash (day 14):
    • Maculopapular, erythematous, blanching rash.
    • Starts behind ears & on face/hairline; spreads downward to neck, trunk, extremities; reaches palms & soles by day 3.
    • Lesions may coalesce; rash becomes brownish & non-blanching by day 4–5; fine desquamation.
    • Rash lasts 5–7 days; fever defervesces as rash peaks.
  • Other features:
    • Generalised lymphadenopathy; splenomegaly.
    • Diarrhoea, vomiting.
    • Conjunctivitis with photophobia; corneal ulceration (vitamin A deficiency — major cause of blindness in measles).
    • Otitis media, pneumonia (viral or secondary bacterial).
    • Encephalitis (~1 in 1000); subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE — rare, late, fatal).

Complications

System Complications
Respiratory
  • Giant cell pneumonia — primary viral; especially in immunocompromised; high mortality.
  • Secondary bacterial pneumonia — S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, S. aureus; most common cause of death.
  • Otitis media — most common complication (5–15%).
  • Laryngotracheobronchitis (croup); bronchiolitis.
  • TB reactivation.
GastrointestinalDiarrhoea, vomiting, dehydration, stomatitis; malnutrition worsens
OcularConjunctivitis; keratitis; corneal ulceration & blindness (especially with vitamin A deficiency); xerophthalmia
Neurological
  • Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) — autoimmune demyelination; ~1 in 1000 cases; 15% mortality; 25–40% neurological sequelae.
  • Measles inclusion body encephalitis (MIBE) — immunocompromised patients; within 6 months of infection; fatal.
  • Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) — rare (1 in 10,000–100,000); 5–15 years after measles; progressive fatal neurodegenerative disease.

Miscarriage, premature birthIn pregnant women with measles
HaematologicalThrombocytopenia; disseminated intravascular coagulation

    • Any person with fever & maculopapular rash (i.e., non-vesicular) AND at least one of cough, coryza, or conjunctivitis.
    • Travel or contact with confirmed case.
  • Koplik spots — pathognomonic clinical sign.

2. Laboratory Confirmation

a) Serology — Most Common
  • Measles-specific IgM ELISA:
    • Indicates recent infection (persists 1–2 months).
    • Appears within 1–2 days of rash; peaks at 7–10 days; persists 4 weeks.
    • Sensitivity 80% on day of rash; 95%+ by day 4–5.
    • Single serum sample sufficient for diagnosis.
    • False negative — early infection (<3 days after rash); repeat after 7–10 days.
    • False positive — recent MMR vaccination (IgM appears in 5–10% of vaccinees, lasting 2–4 weeks).
  • Four-fold rise in IgG titre between paired sera (acute & convalescent 10–14 days apart) — confirms recent infection; useful for retrospective diagnosis.
  • IgG avidity — low avidity indicates recent primary infection; high avidity indicates past infection or vaccination.
b) Viral Detection — PCR
  • RT-PCR:
    • Detects measles RNA in throat swab, nasopharyngeal swab, urine, blood.
    • Most sensitive in prodrome & first few days of rash.
    • Specific — distinguishes wild-type from vaccine strain (genotyping).
    • Useful for outbreak investigation & surveillance.
  • Genotyping — WHO standardised; 24 genotypes; useful for tracking transmission chains; India's endemic genotype is D8.
c) Viral Isolation — Culture
  • Cell culture — Vero, B95a, HEp-2 cells; cytopathic effect (syncytia, giant cells).
  • Specimen — throat swab, nasopharyngeal aspirate, urine (sediment contains infected cells).
  • Slow (1–2 weeks); not routine; useful for research & genotyping.
d) Antigen Detection
  • Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) — measles antigen in nasopharyngeal cells; rapid (hours).
  • Immunohistochemistry — on biopsy or postmortem tissue; detects measles antigen in Warthin-Finkeldey giant cells.
e) Other Tests
  • Complete blood count — leucopenia; lymphopenia; thrombocytopenia.
  • Vitamin A level — low in malnourished; supplement.
  • Chest X-ray — pneumonia pattern; interstitial infiltrates (viral); consolidation (bacterial).
  • EEG, MRI brain — for encephalitis / SSPE.
  • CSF analysis — for encephalitis; lymphocytic pleocytosis; raised protein; measles antibody in CSF (SSPE).
  • Tuberculin test — temporarily negative during & after measles (anergy); re-test 4–6 weeks after recovery.

Treatment

  • No specific antiviral therapy.
  • Supportive care:
    • Rest, hydration, antipyretics (paracetamol — NOT aspirin in children — Reye syndrome).
    • Vitamin A supplementation — WHO recommends for all children with measles; reduces mortality & blindness:
      • 50,000 IU if <6 months.
      • 100,000 IU if 6–12 months.
      • 200,000 IU if >12 months; repeat next day; third dose 4 weeks later if xerophthalmia.
    • Treat secondary bacterial infections — antibiotics (based on culture).
    • Treat diarrhoea — ORS.
    • Eye care — vitamin A, topical antibiotics.
    • Isolation — until 4 days after rash onset (airborne precautions).
  • Severe measles (pneumonia, encephalitis) — ICU; ribavirin (investigational).

Prevention

  • Measles vaccine:
    • Live attenuated — Edmonston-Zagreb strain (India — given subcutaneously); Moraten, Schwarz strains (other countries).
    • Given as MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) or MR (measles-rubella).
    • Schedule (India):
      • MR at 9 months (or 6 months in outbreak setting).
      • MR booster at 16–24 months.
      • India's MR campaign (2017–2019) — mass vaccination of 410 million children 9 months–15 years.
    • Efficacy — 93% after 1 dose; 97% after 2 doses.
    • Contraindicated in pregnancy, severe immunosuppression (HIV with CD4 <15%), severe allergy to neomycin/gelatin.
    • Should not be given within 4 weeks of BCG (interference).
  • Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP):
    • Vaccine within 72 h of exposure — for susceptible contacts; may prevent or modify disease.
    • Immunoglobulin (IVIG or IMIG) within 6 days of exposure — for contacts who cannot receive vaccine (infants <6 months, pregnant women, immunocompromised); 0.5 mL/kg IM (max 15 mL).
  • Herd immunity — requires >95% vaccine coverage (high R₀); below this, outbreaks occur.
  • Surveillance & outbreak investigation — report suspected cases; genotyping to track source.

  • WHO targets measles elimination in 5 of 6 regions by 2020; missed deadline.
  • India — Measles-Rubella (MR) campaign 2017–2019; introduced MR vaccine in UIP (replacing standalone measles).
  • Elimination requires ≥95% coverage with 2 doses; outbreak investigation; case-based surveillance with lab confirmation.
  • Resurgence in 2023–24 due to COVID-19 pandemic vaccination disruption; WHO issued global warning.

Koplik spots are the pathognomonic clinical sign of measles — grayish-white papules on erythematous base on buccal mucosa opposite lower molars; appear 1–2 days before rash; allow early diagnosis during prodrome. The rash starts behind the ears & face, spreads downward — this cephalocaudal spread is characteristic. The 2019 Samoa measles outbreak (87 deaths, mostly children) was triggered by low vaccine coverage from antivaxx messaging. India's MR campaign (2017–2019) vaccinated 410 million children — major step toward elimination; but COVID-19 pandemic disrupted routine immunisation, leading to resurgence in 2023–24. Introduction

Aspergillosis refers to a spectrum of diseases caused by moulds of the genus Aspergillus, most commonly Aspergillus fumigatus (~80% of human infections); also A. flavus, A. niger, A. terreus, A. nidulans. Aspergillus is ubiquitous in environment — soil, decaying vegetation, compost, dust, air conditioning systems. Inhalation of conidia (spores) is the primary route of infection.

Clinical Syndromes

1. Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis (ABPA)

  • Hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus antigens in patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis.
  • Recurrent wheeze, cough, brownish sputum plugs (mucus plugs containing hyphae), fleeting pulmonary infiltrates, eosinophilia.
  • Pathogenesis — IgE-mediated Type I + immune complex Type III hypersensitivity.
  • Diagnosis — Rosenberg-Patterson criteria (asthma, immediate skin reactivity to Aspergillus, total IgE >1000 IU/mL, elevated Aspergillus-specific IgE/IgG, eosinophilia, pulmonary infiltrates, central bronchiectasis).
  • Treatment — oral corticosteroids (prednisolone); itraconazole (antifungal — reduces steroid requirement); omalizumab (anti-IgE) in refractory.

2. Aspergilloma (Fungus Ball / Mycetoma)

  • Colonisation of pre-existing pulmonary cavity (TB, sarcoid, bronchiectasis) by Aspergillus; forms a ball of fungal hyphae mixed with mucus & cellular debris.
  • Often asymptomatic; may cause haemoptysis (sometimes massive & life-threatening — erosion into adjacent bronchial artery); chronic cough.
  • Imaging — chest X-ray / CT: round/oval mass with crescent of air ("air crescent" sign / Monod's sign) within a cavity, typically in upper lobe; gravity-dependent movement on changing position.
  • Serology — Aspergillus precipitating antibody (IgG) positive.
  • Treatment — surgical resection (lobectomy) for significant haemoptysis; antifungals have poor penetration into cavity; bronchial artery embolisation for acute bleeding.

3. Chronic Pulmonary Aspergillosis (CPA / Chronic Necrotising Pulmonary Aspergillosis)

  • Slowly progressive infection in patients with underlying lung disease (COPD, old TB, sarcoidosis) but mild immunocompromise.
  • Subacute course — weeks to months; cough, weight loss, haemoptysis, fever.
  • Imaging — progressive cavity with surrounding infiltrate; pleural thickening.
  • Diagnosis — culture/histology from biopsy; Aspergillus IgG positive; galactomannan may be positive.
  • Treatment — long-term oral itraconazole or voriconazole (≥6 months); surgical resection if localised.

4. Invasive Pulmonary Aspergillosis (IPA) — Most Severe

  • Occurs in severely immunocompromised — neutropenia (<500/µL), haematological malignancy (AML, ALL), stem cell transplant, solid organ transplant, prolonged high-dose steroids, advanced HIV.
  • Angioinvasive — hyphae invade blood vessels → thrombosis, infarction, haemorrhagic necrosis; disseminates haematogenously to brain, heart, kidney, liver, skin, GI.
  • Clinical — fever (often refractory to broad-spectrum antibiotics), pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, dyspnoea, cough; may mimic pulmonary embolism.
  • Imaging — CT chest: halo sign (nodular lesion surrounded by ground-glass opacity — haemorrhage); later air crescent sign (cavitation as neutrophils recover); multiple nodules.
  • Diagnosis — galactomannan antigen (serum, BAL); PCR; culture; histopathology (biopsy).
  • Treatment — voriconazole IV/PO (drug of choice; reduces mortality vs amphotericin); isavuconazole; amphotericin B lipid formulation; caspofungin ( salvage); echinocandin. Reverse immunosuppression if possible.
  • Mortality 40–60% even with treatment; >90% untreated.

5. Invasive Sinus Aspergillosis

  • Acute invasive — in immunocompromised; similar to mucormycosis; rapidly progressive; angioinvasive; orbital cellulitis, cranial nerve palsy, cerebral extension.
  • Chronic invasive — in immunocompetent / diabetic; slowly progressive sinus disease; bony erosion.
  • Aspergillus granuloma (paranasal sinus fungus ball) — non-invasive mass of hyphae in sinus; chronic sinusitis; surgical removal.
  • Treatment — surgical debridement + antifungal (voriconazole).

6. Disseminated Aspergillosis

  • Haematogenous spread from lung; brain (cerebral aspergillosis — ring-enhancing lesions, stroke, abscess); heart (endocarditis); skin (multiple papules, nodules, eschars); kidney; liver; GI.
  • Often fatal.

7. Other Forms

  • Aspergillus endocarditis — prosthetic valve; culture-negative; large friable vegetations; emboli.
  • Cerebral aspergillosis — ring-enhancing lesion; haemorrhagic infarct; abscess; high mortality.
  • Cutaneous aspergillosis — primary (traumatic inoculation); secondary (disseminated); necrotising skin lesions.
  • Otomycosis — Aspergillus (especially A. niger — black tufts) in external auditory canal; pruritus, discharge; topical antifungal.
  • Keratitis — corneal infection; trauma, contact lens; Aspergillus; topical natamycin, amphotericin.
  • Onychomycosis — nail infection; A. niger.
  • Gastrointestinal aspergillosis — rare; in neutropenia; ulceration, bleeding, perforation.

Pathogenesis

  • Conidia (spores) inhaled; small size (2–3 µm) allows reach alveoli.
  • Adhesion — conidia adhere to epithelial cells & extracellular matrix (laminin, fibrinogen).
  • Germination — conidia germinate into hyphae at 37 °C; hyphae invade tissue.
  • Angioinvasion — hyphae invade blood vessels (especially in immunocompromised); thrombosis, infarction, haematogenous dissemination.
  • Virulence factors:
    • Galactomannan — cell wall polysaccharide; released during growth; diagnostic marker.
    • β-1,3-glucan — cell wall component.
    • Pigments (melanin, gliotoxin) — antioxidant; immune evasion; cytotoxic (apoptosis of immune cells).
    • Proteases, elastases, phospholipases — tissue invasion.
    • Siderophores — iron acquisition.
    • Aflatoxin (A. flavus) — carcinogen; not directly related to aspergillosis.
  • Host defences — macrophages (ingest conidia); neutrophils (kill hyphae via oxidative burst, NETs); T cells (Th1, Th17).

Laboratory Diagnosis

1. Specimen

  • Sputum, BAL (bronchoalveolar lavage), tracheal aspirate.
  • Blood — serum for galactomannan, β-D-glucan; PCR; (blood culture usually negative — angioinvasive but does not septate in blood).
  • Tissue biopsy — lung, sinus, brain, skin.
  • CSF — for cerebral aspergillosis (galactomannan, PCR; culture usually negative).
  • Ear swab — otomycosis.
  • Corneal scrape — keratitis.

2. Direct Microscopy

  • KOH mount / Calcofluor white — septate hyphae, acute-angle (45°) branching; 3–6 µm wide; characteristic of Aspergillus (also seen in other hyaline moulds — Fusarium, Scedosporium — cannot distinguish).
  • Contrast with Mucorales — broad (6–15 µm), ribbon-like, aseptate (pauciseptate), right-angle (90°) branching.
  • Gram stain — may show hyphae.
  • Histopathology — septate acute-angle hyphae invading tissue; GMS (Grocott methenamine silver) or PAS stain; angioinvasion; necrosis.

3. Culture

  • Sabouraud dextrose agar (SDA) — without cycloheximide (inhibits Aspergillus); incubate at 25–30 °C for 3–7 days.
  • Blood agar, potato dextrose agar, Czapek-Dox agar.
  • Colony morphology:
    • A. fumigatus — smoky green to grey-green colonies; velvety or powdery; reverse white to tan.
    • A. flavus — yellow-green (olive); also produces aflatoxin.
    • A. niger — black colonies (carbon black); white reverse; common in otomycosis.
    • A. terreus — cinnamon-brown; amphotericin B resistant.
    • A. nidulans — green to buff.

4. Microscopic Identification

  • Lactophenol cotton blue mount — reveals conidiophore structure:
    • Foot cell — basal hyphal cell from which conidiophore arises.
    • Conidiophore (vesicle) — swollen at tip.
    • Phialides — bottle-shaped cells; may cover entire vesicle (A. fumigatus — uniseriate, upper half only) or be in two rows (biseriate — A. flavus, A. niger).
    • Conidia — chains of small round spores; cover vesicle ("spore head").
  • A. fumigatus — uniseriate; phialides on upper half of vesicle; columnar spore chains.
  • A. niger — biseriate; phialides cover entire vesicle; large globular head; black conidia.
  • A. flavus — biseriate; phialides cover entire vesicle; yellow-green conidia.

5. Antigen Detection

  • Galactomannan (GM) antigen:
    • Aspergillus cell wall polysaccharide; released during growth.
    • Serum — sensitivity 70–85%, specificity 90–95%; 2 samples/week in high-risk patients.
    • BAL — higher sensitivity (80–90%); cut-off index ≥0.5 (serum) or ≥1.0 (BAL).
    • CSF — for cerebral aspergillosis.
    • False positive — piperacillin-tazobactam, amoxicillin-clavulanate (historical — formulations now improved); cross-reactivity with other moulds (Penicillium, Fusarium, Histoplasma); Gluconobacter bacteraemia; neonates; double-fraction wheat.
    • False negative — antifungal prophylaxis (reduces fungal load).
  • β-D-glucan:
    • Cell wall component shared with Candida, Fusarium, Pneumocystis — NOT specific for Aspergillus.
    • Useful screening for invasive fungal infection; 2 serial positives.
    • False positive — haemodialysis, IVIG, albumin, gauze.

6. Molecular Tests

  • PCR — Aspergillus DNA in blood, BAL, CSF, tissue; targets 18S rRNA, 28S rRNA, ITS region; sensitivity & specificity vary.
  • Real-time PCR — quantitative; faster.
  • Combined galactomannan + PCR improves diagnostic accuracy.

7. Other Tests

  • Skin test — Aspergillus antigen; immediate hypersensitivity (Type I) for ABPA diagnosis.
  • Serology:
    • Total IgE — elevated in ABPA (>1000 IU/mL).
    • Aspergillus-specific IgE — ABPA.
    • Aspergillus precipitating antibody (IgG) — aspergilloma, CPA; positive in 90%.
    • Aspergillus-specific IgG ELISA — chronic pulmonary aspergillosis.
  • Imaging:
    • Chest CT — halo sign (early); air crescent sign (late); nodules; consolidation; cavitation.
    • Chest X-ray — non-specific.
    • Sinus CT — bony erosion, sinus opacity.
    • Brain MRI — ring-enhancing lesions; haemorrhagic infarct.
  • Bronchoscopy — BAL for microscopy, culture, galactomannan, PCR; transbronchial biopsy for histopathology.

EORTC/MSG Diagnostic Criteria for Invasive Aspergillosis

Definite — histopathology + culture from sterile site. Probable — host factor + clinical feature + mycological evidence. Possible — host factor + clinical feature alone.

Treatment

Syndrome First-line Alternatives
Invasive aspergillosisVoriconazole IV/PO — drug of choiceIsavuconazole; liposomal amphotericin B; caspofungin (salvage); posaconazole
ABPAPrednisolone + ItraconazoleOmalizumab; voriconazole

  • Prophylaxis in high-risk patients (neutropenia, transplant) — posaconazole, itraconazole, voriconazole; aerosolised amphotericin B.
  • Protected environments — HEPA-filtered rooms; positive pressure; avoid plants/flowers.
  • Avoid dust exposure — construction sites; gardening (mask if gardening).
  • Reverse immunosuppression — reduce steroids; G-CSF for neutropenia.
  • Surveillance — galactomannan twice weekly in high-risk.

Clinical Pearl

The halo sign on CT chest (nodule surrounded by ground-glass opacity) in a neutropenic patient is highly suggestive of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis — start voriconazole empirically while awaiting confirmation. The air crescent sign (crescent of air around a nodular lesion) develops later — indicates cavitation as neutrophils recover & infarcted tissue separates from viable lung; heralds neutrophil recovery. Galactomannan antigen (serum & BAL) is the key non-culture diagnostic test — sensitivity 70–85% in serum, 80–90% in BAL; positive in serum of high-risk patient = probable invasive aspergillosis. Voriconazole is the drug of choice for invasive aspergillosis — superior to amphotericin B (Herbrecht et al. 2002 NEJM trial — improved survival). Always reverse immunosuppression — reduce steroids, G-CSF for neutropenia; without immune recovery, antifungals alone often fail. Aspergilloma (fungus ball) — surgical resection is definitive treatment for symptomatic haemoptysis; antifungals do NOT penetrate cavity well. COVID-associated pulmonary aspergillosis (CAPA) — emerging complication of severe COVID-19 (especially ICU patients on steroids); high mortality; galactomannan + BAL culture for diagnosis.
